The spirit that now brings you joy, so that you may spend your courage in slandering and reviling me, might well become hellfire for you and enter your conscience. Where will you remain then?

You drive me to tears and earnest prayer against your blasphemy while you accuse me entirely with falsehoods. Take heed that my tears do not become burning coals upon your head. I have prayed much to GOD for you, that GOD might enlighten you and grant you knowledge of the truth. But you only grow worse with your slandering; I will remain innocent before you, should the wrath of GOD touch you.

Dear Herr <term>Primarius</term> <gloss>senior church official</gloss>, why do you despise me because I am a <term>Lay</term> <gloss>layperson/unlearned person</gloss> and possess divine and natural knowledge? Do you believe that the <term>H. Geist</term> <gloss>Holy Spirit</gloss> is bound to your schools? Did not Christ, our beloved, say, "My Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him for it"? Likewise: "Ask, and you shall receive; knock, and it shall be opened unto you," etc.

I have received my gift through earnest asking and knocking, and have tasted something that I would not trade for all the honor and wealth of the world, and which I can never deny. Why do you attribute the gift of GOD to the devil? Look back into the world and see how often GOD has used simple people for His work.

You do not understand it, and it was not written for the pulpit, nor was it meant to come before the public. He wrote another book on the occasion of the controversies that arose in England between missionaries of the secular and regular clergy. In order to settle these, Richard Smith, Bishop of Chalcedon, was sent by Urban VIII. He seemed to favor the regulars less and even to disturb rather than promote their ministries. Hence arose complaints and various pamphlets, two of which were accused of attacking episcopal authority or at least showing it too little deference. Sancyranus <note>a reference to Jean du Vergier de Hauranne, Abbé de Saint-Cyran</note> seized this opportunity to declaim against the regulars and issued that famous pamphlet on the *Hierarchy* under the pseudonym of *Petrus Aurelius*. The work was well-received as long as the author remained hidden, and it was approved by the Synod of the Gallican Clergy on April 27, 1641, and committed to the press at their expense. Antoine Godeau, Bishop of Grasse, added a eulogy in which the author is proclaimed an "invincible defender of bishops, a most fierce lover of the truth, a most just vindicator of the Hierarchy, and a theologian raised in the bosom of ancestral theology." Sancyranus's modesty did not have enough strength to allow him to remain hidden any longer amidst such commendation of himself and his work. But when the author was discovered, a blush covered their faces, and all that pomp of words eventually vanished even from the book *Gallia Christiana*.

Indeed, he proved himself a candidate of ancestral theology in the book condemned on April 23, 1654: *Familiar Theology, or a brief explanation of the mysteries of the Faith*

It is easy to divine with what sense of grief the faction saw its nest disturbed so suddenly. First there was huge trepidation, then outcries: hence the torments and mournful laments of those deploring the persecution of truth and innocence; hence the curses, devoting whatever was of sacred and profane dignity: finally, there was an uproar among the very parts of the faction, and a struggle continued for many years into the present century. Finally, the Archbishop of Mechelen, Humbertus Guil. a Precipiano, after he had subjected another priest of the Oratory, Van Hame, to canonical penalties in the year 1700 for spreading inferior principles of faith despite repeated warnings, and had initiated action against Quesnel in Rome in the year 1702, seized Gerberon—who had been extracted from the furthest corner of the city of Brussels—in the year 1703, after more certain evidence of their hideouts had been reported the previous year. Quesnel himself, along with his inseparable companion Brigode, who, although warned by Roman letters to depart the city, had merely changed his lodgings and retreated to a house called the *Refuge de Forest* <gloss>Refuge of the Forest</gloss>, was apprehended there. Through the help of his companion, he had already escaped the hands of the imminent officers, but, recalled by the memory of the papers which it was of the greatest importance to keep from the eyes of men, he was intercepted by the hidden guards in the month of May and was brought to the Palace of the Prelate on the Wednesday after Pentecost.

Quesnel remained there for no more than three months. For his fellow clansmen, as they explored every crack to find a way to offer him aid, finally signaled to Ernest, a Canon of Saint Gudula, with a note pulled by a lead weight from the windows, informing him of the location, position, and condition of his custody. They pierced the wall with labor continued over two nights, and thus, on September 13th, after midnight, they restored their precious head to liberty, and he soon rushed away into Holland. All of his papers that were intercepted showed what he had prepared to disturb the peace of the Church. But neither could these turbulent minds remain hidden for long in Belgium. They were detected in the year 1690 by Castanaga, the Governor of Belgium, and ordered to leave Brussels. They complied without delay and went to Leiden in the month of April. However, having changed their plans shortly thereafter, they departed for the territory of Liège and settled near a certain castle. Finding themselves less secure there, they soon entered the city itself and kept themselves there until the end of August, known to very few. When they grew weary of being tossed about, they disregarded the danger and returned secretly to Brussels after six months, seeking their old hiding places, from which, by the testimony of Quesnel himself in certain of his letters, they did not set foot for the entire four years that Arnauld survived. During this time, Quesnel polished his work, and Arnauld, with his assistance, sought to exert his final strength against the Bulls of the Popes and against the recent Decree of Alexander VIII, by which 31 propositions and many of Arnauld’s own were condemned, in a book written as *Difficulties Proposed Against Doctor Steyart of Leuven*. Having finished this labor, the old man, a bridge-jumper <note>a metaphorical term for one at the end of their life, ready to cross over</note> of 82 years, having received the viaticum <note>the Eucharist given to one in danger of death</note> from the hands of Quesnel, expired on August 8, 1694.

From what source, I do not know, and he fashions a remarkable eulogy, which it will not be out of place to append below, illustrated with notes; it reads as follows.

> In the year 1699, on the 17th day before the Kalends of September <note>August 16th</note>, died in the territory of Liège Antoine Arnauld, a Frenchman and Doctor of the Sorbonne, a man regarded by many with ambiguous <note>(a)</note> fame. This is because he maintained with full vigor <note>(b)</note> in many writings <note>(c)</note> that the grace of God is efficacious in itself <note>(d)</note>, contrary to those who attacked it, with the errors condemned in Cornelius Jansen being imputed to him <note>(e)</note>, which he professed in his final breath to condemn with sincere judgment along with the Catholic Church <note>(f)</note>. He was a man whose integrity of morals <note>(g)</note> was not unequal to his learning, which he displayed, enduring <note>(h)</note> slanders and exiles with equal zeal and patience, with a spirit <note>(i)</note> always unconquered and docile <note>(k)</note>. He wrote many books filled with sacred erudition <note>(l)</note>, especially in defense of the Most Holy Eucharist, whose faith and reverence he defended forcefully against the heterodox <note>(m)</note> and the nibblers at the sacred table <note>(n)</note>. Yet, having experienced <note>(o)</note> no more placated spirits toward him on the part of some, in order to withdraw himself from their harassment, he turned into a secret solitude, where he grew old amid meditations and writing; by the judgment of Innocent XI (restrain your laughter), he was at one time to be co-opted among the Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, had not human reason persuaded that this sacrifice should be taken for the sake of the peace of the Church (suppress your anger) to be bought off from his harassers <note>(p)</note>.

These things the anonymous author records in the Appendix of a Jesuit book—he pursues Nicole, Codde the Bishop of Sebaste, and others with a similar eulogy. You will recognize the bird by its song.

And with these, all the Duke’s plans conceived in his mind for bringing the Cardinal back to the path were finally overturned.

Meanwhile the Appellants triumphed, though not without grief for the death of Quesnel, their leader most esteemed after Arnauld, from whom all this present cause was derived. It is not pleasing here to weave the history of this man’s life; it is helpful to add only two things worthy of memory to what has already been said about him. The first is a certain writing sent by Quesnel himself to a certain Priest, who, having at last wiped away the darkness of errors, was returned to himself and the Church, and produced it. These were rules comprised in 12 articles, which his own were to use in conversation among themselves and with various kinds of men. The sum was almost this: Union and concord: faith in the secret: circumspection in speech according to the varying condition of men: ambiguity <note>original: "amphibologia"</note> in various heads of Religion: he wished it to be said that they use Christ present in the Eucharist, not only by faith or figure, as the heterodox do, but neither by transubstantiation or substantially or really, as Catholics say: how then? in an imperceptible manner. In the Sacrament of penance, they were to urge the insufficiency of attrition <note>sorrow for sin based on fear of punishment</note> and the necessity of perfect contrition <note>sorrow for sin based on love of God</note>. That they should openly impugn sufficient grace, the liberty of indifference, and merits, and at other times through the vagueness of words, so that a way out might be open to the pressed: that they should uniquely extol victorious grace: and thus many other things. Quesnel, when asked by his nephew Pinfon, a sculptor, to which side in the then-litigious matters of religion he should lean, replied by letter: "He should hold himself to the greater part of the faithful, or firmly adhere to the trunk of the Church; for he himself had been provoked and compelled to foster these disputes so stubbornly only by the injuries of the Jesuits." Pinfon affirmed that he had heard the same thing before him, and not just once, from the mouth of Quesnel himself, as attested by the Bishop of Angers, Poncet de la Rivière, in his <term>Reflexiones consolatoriæ</term> <gloss>Consolatory Reflections</gloss>. But from the time that madness seized the man, in the year 1719, when he was brought to the brink of death at an advanced age in Amsterdam, four days before he died, having called two witnesses, he renewed his appeal, and thus, having received viaticum from his pastor, the old man lived until the 2nd of December, at the age of 85.

Furthermore, the fruits of these disturbances were most sorrowful. Noailles was further terrified by the Council of Embrun and by the authority of the King in defending its acts. In the year 1727, several bishops had gathered at Embrun to overthrow the immense errors that were being spread everywhere by the schismatics and to settle the disturbances stirred up by them. Indeed, the obstinacy of this man could not be overcome. Therefore, by the sentence of the Council, he was forbidden from every function, both Episcopal and Priestly, and a Vicar General was appointed for his diocese. It would be long to recount the outcries and tumults that this scene produced. Twelve Bishops protested against this sentence and brought a formal objection to the King himself. Fifty advocates of the Parisian Court signed a consultation concerning the nullity of the sentence and the acts of the Council of Embrun. Answer. And that manner, or the mouth suitable for eating the flesh of Christ itself, is faith. What then? Osiander is deceived, and indeed childishly, who thinks that the flesh of Christ itself is different, or is eaten differently, in spiritual manducation than in sacramental. But if the flesh of Christ is the same, then it is received with the same mouth, with the same teeth, with the same stomach: namely, spiritually, not corporally: by faith, not by the mouth: by the spirit, not by the belly. We confess indeed that Christ, as he is God, can do all things: but because he can neither lie, nor be contrary to himself, he does not wish to destroy his own flesh, which he wishes to possess forever: and he who wishes it to be truly human and bodily flesh, does not wish it to be non-human flesh. Which, however, must necessarily follow, if he were to station this flesh of his as everywhere present at the same time and simultaneously.

*The Son of God performs his actions and operations through his assumed humanity, just as in the human body the soul perfects its actions through its body. Therefore, since the Son of God works everywhere, it must be that his flesh is present everywhere.* Answer. In this place, Osiander <note>original: Osiander</note> rehashes and casts back at us the first argument of the Apollinarian <note>original: Apolinaristarum</note> heretics, who attributed Deity to the flesh of Christ, just as a soul is attributed to a body. Furthermore, the very likeness used by Osiander overturns the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ. For just as a soul, even though hypostatically united to a body, does not exercise all its operations through the body, such as meditating, reasoning, and the like: so too the Deity of Christ does not perfect all its actions through his humanity, even after the union. Therefore, it does not conclude that it is present everywhere.

<margin>Page 28.</margin> *The humanity assumed by Christ is one person with his own Deity, and is hypostatically united with it. Therefore, wherever the Deity of Christ is, there also is his flesh or humanity.* Answer. First, this man formerly took the presence of Christ in the Lord’s Supper <note>original: Cœna Domini</note> not from the hypostatic union, but from these words of Christ: "This is my body." Next, recognizing that this protection of his is weak, he now abandons it, and turns himself toward the hypostatic union.

<summary>This page continues the refutation of Lucas Osiander’s arguments for the omnipresence of Christ's physical body, specifically addressing his use of the hypostatic union to justify the ubiquity of Christ's humanity.</summary>

For it is not food for the belly, but for the mind: nor is it taken by the mouth, but by faith, and spiritual things require spiritual instruments. Therefore, what is said by that man, that Judas, the betrayer of the Lord, took and ate the very body of Christ, but to his own destruction, is false. For the body of Christ is entirely life-giving to anyone who eats it. How, then, is the flesh of Christ to anyone for their destruction? It is so when it is despised, but not when it is taken and eaten. For it is death when despised, but not when taken. Therefore, Judas took the bread of the Lord, that is, the sacrament and sign of the body of the Lord: but not the bread [that is] the Lord, that is, the very true body of Christ, because it is always life-giving, just as Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo, influential early Christian theologian</note> excellently said.

<margin>Page 39.</margin> *Christ called that very thing which he gave to Judas Iscariot his body, and which Judas took. Therefore, Judas took the very body of Christ.* R. The bread itself is a sacrament, and is called the body of Christ sacramentally: and the essential body of Christ is also called the body of Christ, but not sacramentally, rather naturally. Therefore, these appellations should not be confused, and what was said by Christ regarding the bread sacramentally is not to be understood regarding the very body of Christ itself, which Osiander does here with great error.

Furthermore, Zipporah did not circumcise the children of others, but only her own. And yet, Osiander permits this to women as if they were midwives (as appears from their custom and practice), so that they may even baptize the children of others. What, therefore, does the example of Zipporah contribute to Osiander’s opinion, when the opposite is rather gathered from it? Namely, that even if a man is present, a woman may be able to baptize, not anyone’s children, but only her own. This, therefore, is our first response to this example of Zipporah. The second, however, is that he gathers a general principle from a particular instance, and establishes a perpetual rule from an extraordinary act, when we read nowhere else that women among the people of God, and under the law, circumcised their own or others' children. Moreover, this was also to the great insult and reproach of Moses himself. For the Lord, by that means, accused Moses through his wife of excessive negligence, because he had not circumcised his sons, and had neglected that sacrosanct covenant of God with his family by omitting circumcision. Finally, who does not see that the nature of Baptism and Circumcision was different in this regard? For we nowhere read that the duty of circumcision was once commanded by God specifically to the priests, since circumcision was both instituted by God and practiced by the people for more than four hundred years before the priests were separated from the rest of the people. The fifth mode of discerning is if there is weight of humility in the deeds, words, gestures, and manners of that spirit, just as weight is wont to be grasped in a coin. For instance, if the wailing, groaning, complaint, petition, recognition of sins, or confession of guilt or of penalties is heard from him or similar things, such that there is no glorification, boasting, domination, blasphemy, or disparagement or cursing. For it must be believed that this spirit conducts itself after the manner of a beggar, who laments his defects, begging for aid and alms from the living. And this is a sign of good hope, and one should believe it is permitted to him by a special grace from God, because perhaps he has no other consolation except the common suffrages of the church, to whom God has mercifully granted that he may also beg for special ones. For the virtue of humility, in whoever it may appear, cannot be without grace, the scripture saying: "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." You will find nothing fatal in me. **G**regory also, in a certain homily, seems to hint that [the devil] was not absent even from Christ as he died, concerning the words: **T**he prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me <note>John 14:30</note>. **A**nd Bede seems to hold the same, that Satan was not absent when he was hanging on the cross. **I**n other revelations, too, we read how demons were seen present around the dying, just as the same Gregory reports concerning the rich man Chrysoreus, who was given over to a worldly and carnal life, who saw them standing by him on all sides, and finally snatching his soul away to the infernal regions. **T**heir faces are so horrible, as those who have seen them report, that they would rather choose to be thrown into a furnace of burning fire than to look at or behold them for a single blink of an eye. <note>Rubricated paragraph mark</note> How hard it will be for the damned to burn forever in the fire with such beings. **I**t seems, therefore, from the perversity of the demons, that by the common law they leave no one untempted, nor do they permit them to die in peace, unless divine clemency reserves our fragility. **T**hey would even intrude themselves visibly if angelic

As Cyril reports, writing to Augustine regarding Saint Eusebius, a disciple of the blessed Jerome, with what infestation they attacked him as he was dying, whom they compelled to despair and deny God. Horrendous things are also read about the three resurrected at the death of Saint Jerome. The remedy, therefore, against demons around the dying does not seem more effective than the presence of devout people in prayers, and reading aloud the passions of Christ from the Gospels, and the creeds, and the litany. Hearing these, the demons flee, as Gregory reports in a homily about a certain worldly man living in a secular manner in a monastery, who, when he had come to the hour of death, saw a dragon coming toward him and absorbing his head into its mouth, and he cried out to the religious brothers present, saying,</meta>

> Behold, I am given to the dragon to be devoured. On account of your presence, it cannot devour me. If I am given to it, why do I suffer delays because of you?

**To whom the brothers replied,**

> Impress the sign of the cross upon yourself.

**To whom he replied,**

> I want to, but I cannot, because I am bound by the dragon.

**Then the brothers, falling to the ground,** 
began to pray, and so the dragon retreated. Behold, the prayers of the devout around the dying are of great value. But, therefore, after the soul's departure from the body, they will soon go to a particular judgment; it may be doubted to what place they are led where they are judged. For it is not to be believed that all are led upward to heaven, waiting for the sentence there, especially the reprobate, and that immediately upon the sentence being received, it is pronounced to the infernal regions. For the dignity of the place and the indignity of the perverse soul do not allow this to be done, but rather right reason. Thus, neither [is it to be believed] concerning souls being purged, that they slip back from heaven to purgatory below. Vecturius, a man (as you know) formerly considered one of the most affluent of citizens, had his affairs poorly managed and contracted a large amount of debt. And he had kept this hidden, both from those who were his necessary associates and from those who loved the man. What he did afterward, when it was no longer possible to assist his fortune further, would perhaps have been understood in a few years. Having collected his goods from everywhere as secretly as he could, he pretended to go abroad and promised to arrive early on the first day of August, on the very Kalends. He urged all of us who loved him to stand as guarantors for him, in case anyone should happen to summon him to court. We thought, however, that he was held by no, or at most a very small, debt. And even if he were held by a large one, we thought he was solvent. What more? I provided surety for him. Then, he departed. When the day for the repayment of the debt arrived, and that man did not appear as he should have in good faith on the appointed day, we were shortly after demanded for satisfaction by the creditors. When we inquired about him and asked the judges to extend the day for us, and I learned that this would be ordered against us, it became necessary to pay on his behalf. That sum of money which he owed to his creditors was paid out. Even though this matter happened very inconveniently for the others, it was nevertheless so burdensome that I never hope to be able to pay off the debt which I contracted for his sake. I never would have thought it possible that that man could have come to such poverty, or that he would attack his own people with machinations and deceits of this kind. You do this on account of your benevolence toward me, which is great, and I give you the greatest thanks. But I would have you know that I am little moved in spirit by this loss of yours, just as if the damage had been done in part to my own fortune. For I have always judged regarding you that nothing could happen to you that was not my own, which I believe I have seen clearly for a long time on your behalf. And the time is not far off when I might show my mind to you if the opportunity were present. But since our homeland has been worn out and almost destroyed by continuous wars, and the income from the fields does not respond to the landlords, and those arts are not practiced in the city by which the citizens formerly made great profit and wealth, all things have indeed abandoned the seekers of profit. And among those who have resources and money, there is no one, however, who would not prefer to keep their affairs in port than to commit themselves to manifest dangers. If there is anything, however, in which I can be of service to you with any zeal or my own effort, I will do all things with a good spirit, which I understand to be for your use. Nor do I wish your duty to be understood in these matters which pertain to you. In other matters, however, I will use your prudence. I cannot assist you with money. But I will not hesitate to provide satisfaction and make myself a guarantor for you, and to pledge all my possessions if I understand that such is your will and if there is a need for me to pay on your behalf.

Having been sufficiently informed about this matter by them, I betook myself to Alexandria. Having disposed of your first shipments and having taken care of everything regarding my own affairs that I knew pertained to yours, I ensured that I did not leave idle the time which was very short for your other business. I gathered packages from all sides, and those that were most ready for sailing, I brought into the port. Regarding those on the Ides of March, when they had already placed everything in the ship, the sailors set out from the port, and since the winds were favorable, almost all set their sails at the same time. What followed from there was reported to me not long after. Scarcely two or three ships at most had reached the shore, if any of them were yours. The others, however, as it was said, suffered shipwreck. I suspect that because of the fear of the storm, they had not yet moved from that port, and that they will make the journey to us as soon as that storm has subsided. May our news turn out well. I wished these things to be known to you first through our triremes, so that you might be more informed about all your affairs and might set aside any anxiety if perhaps you had contracted any from this shipwreck. It is not a new thing you write to me, nor is it unknown to me. For how many times, do you believe, have I endured the indignity of such fortune, when I have often seen other citizens and distinguished men similarly stripped of their rights, even though they had sustained the good and the fair? I would prefer, however, that you seek assistance for this disturbance from your own wisdom rather than from common custom. For I know this will be the case: that nothing will more relieve your grief than the fact that none of these things has happened to you through your own merit. And the opinion you hold of your situation will change if you take into account the greater woes of others, rather than the disturbance that is still fresh. But you do not write to me in this desperate matter for the sake of protection or advice, but because it helps you to speak with me about your troubles. You act as friends are accustomed to do. I am accustomed to do the same, knowing that the mind is unburdened. I see that I have laid down the greater part of my vexations when I have opened all my perturbation to my friends. I rejoice greatly in this, and I give you thanks that you have chosen me from among many to whom you might entrust your cares. By these and other signs, and also by this, I judge that I am greatly loved by you. The fourteenth principal also is reserved to the Pope, concerning temporal lords who force others to celebrate divine services in a place under interdict, or who, through heralds, cause the people to be cleared out in order to hear them, or who prohibit those who are publicly excommunicated or under interdict from leaving the churches after being warned to do so when mass is being celebrated, or who, when they themselves are warned, do not leave; they are excommunicated in the <term>Clementines</term>, regarding the sentence of excommunication, chapter <term>quis</term> <gloss>who</gloss>. 

The fifteenth principal is in the <term>Clementines</term>, regarding usury, containing all six cases. First, cities and officials who enact usury are excommunicated. Second, those who dictate them. Third, those who write statutes concerning usury to be paid, not to be reclaimed, or not to be restored. Fourth, those who judge according to those statutes. Fifth, those who do not delete them from the books of the city if they are able within three months. Sixth, those who assist in these matters. These are all excommunicated. Likewise, those who incur the sentence are the powers, captains, rectors, consuls, judges, councilors, or other officials of those cities who attempt the aforementioned things. 

The sixteenth principal contains six in the <term>Clementines</term>, regarding blood relations and affinity, chapter unique: first, one who contracts marriage in a forbidden degree of blood relation; second, in a forbidden degree of affinity; third, with a nun; these are excommunicated. The same applies to religious persons doing this, and to nuns, and also to clerics established in holy orders. These are again three other cases. And the <term>Gloss</term> states that this is established in the aforementioned cases only.

nor do they help, nor do they consent in any way if something is given to them from the robbery or theft, and they knowingly accept, or eat thereof, or clothe themselves, or put it to other uses; they are held to restitution. Regarding such persons, however, who had received something as a gift and had consumed it before they understood the truth of the matter, they are not held to restore it. 

Similarly, an exception is made when someone handles the cause of those despoiled by admonishing and inducing the robber himself to make restitution by his own power, especially if he has a probable hope for the correction of the despoilers, and when he is made powerless to restore in whole or in part through the consumption of such goods by the robber. Those who admonish, therefore, who insist at opportune hours so that the robber might restore the stolen goods, are not held to make restitution. 

Under the second case, likewise, those who know or probably believe that, because of their own following or association with the robbers, or because of their own encouragement or disparagement, the robbers did not do more than they would have done otherwise, and yet they had and spent something from the stolen goods, such persons are held to make restitution for those things held or spent, and also for every damage that they or any of their family caused directly or occasionally. 

The third [case is] when several perform damage together, and even if one without the other, or several without this one, would have done it, such a person is held to pay pro rata, that is, for his own portion. This is how much he burdens him regarding the total damage, if it is not possible to distinguish the damage that he himself inflicted from that which others inflicted. In this, however, an estimation must be made so that he who is more energetic, and he who struck greater fear and terror into the victims, may also be held more. 

Likewise, in the case when some associate themselves with robbers and believe that even without their own assistance or instigation the robbers would have done the damage, they are only held for that which they probably believe the robbers did because of their own instigation or assistance. 

The fourth [case is] if some associate themselves with robbers and do not cooperate with them in doing any damage, [but] are nonetheless prepared in their mind to defend [them] if by chance those to be despoiled had wanted to defend their things from the plunderers, and because of their presence and that of their associates, they did not dare to resist the despoilers.

Otherwise, if they did not go together but each was doing damage separately, each is held for that which he did. Understand this beyond what has already been said, because one without the other would not dare or be able to do the damage; otherwise, each is held even for the part of the damage that he intended. <note>A red paragraph mark begins the sixth and seventh rules.</note>

The sixth rule: let the confessor about to hear women beware, lest while he purges their souls of vices, he himself becomes soiled by voluntary delights. Let him not be a cloth that becomes dirty while washing others, but let him be like a hand that shines while cleaning others. Therefore, let him not believe himself to be a respecter of persons. When he listens to the beautiful or young in confession, he should not assume he is free from danger, nor should he think that because he listens to old women, he is safe. Rather, he should protect himself with good and holy imaginations. 

First, by considering that he ought to be an angel of God and a vicar of God trembling at the judgment. Then, when he turns his eyes or mind from the verses or closing of the confession toward the women, he should see their souls not with the eyes of the body, but with the eyes of the mind; he should see them as representing the image of God, yet leprous or wounded by the dire wounds of mortal sins, or at least wrinkled or scabrous from venial offenses, which must be healed by the blood of Christ and the sacraments of penance. 

Secretly, let the confessor mark himself with the cross, pressing his thumb a little, for the sake of preserving purity. Let him recite at least a short prayer or invocation to God. He should avoid useless chatter and sweet words, which are unnecessary. In this way, he should focus solely on the honor of God and the salvation of the soul of another, with firm intent. Nor should he despair if he is tempted while resisting the delight of the flesh, mindful of the words of Christ to the disciples: "If they drink any deadly thing, it will not hurt them" <note>Mark 16:18</note>. 

He removes the appearance of evil, etc. Regarding this, the blessed Gregory says: priests remove malice from the hearts of others by their good exhortations, they remove the appearance of evil, and while they hear of pestiferous situations and are tempted to pray for the wicked, it is a deadly thing that they drink, but it will not hurt them. The same is consulted in his *Pastoral Care* where he says: It happens often that while the rector's soul recognizes the temptations of another, he himself is struck by the heard temptations; yet these are in no way to be feared by the pastor, because he quickly snatches himself away, and even if he is fatigued by the temptations of others through mercy, he shows the causes of this. Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> says the same in the fourth book <note>referring to his Commentary on the Sentences, Book IV</note>, stating that the prayer one gives in the sacrament of penance restores one, even if some inclination to sin comes from the circumstance of the conversation, that is, from necessarily spoken carnal matters, either in the one confessing or in the confessor. 

The seventh rule: the confessor should not look at the face of the one confessing, especially if she is a woman, lest the one confessing blush, and lest he be wounded in his soul by a woman, the spiritual surgeon <note>The Latin text "cyrologi" appears to be a truncated or garbled form of *chirurgus*, meaning surgeon or healer.</note>.

<summary>This passage provides instructions for confessors regarding the spiritual hazards of hearing confessions, particularly those of women, advising them to maintain internal purity and focus on the soul rather than the body.</summary>
<keywords>Confessio, poenitentia, confessarius, temptation, spiritual purity, Johannes Nider, Manuale confessorum</keywords>

Whence the gloss on that passage in Genesis: "She saw the wood was delectable to the eye" <note>Genesis 3:6</note>, says: "Lest we slip in thought, we must not gaze upon what is not permitted to be desired. For as a clean mind in thought is drawn away from the lascivious pleasure of its own will, our eyes should be as if certain robbers of guilt. For Eve would not have touched the wood unless she had first looked upon it imprudently." It must be considered how much we ought to restrain ourselves from illicit things; for we live in a mortal state, if the matter of the living comes to death through the eyes.

The eighth rule: the confessor should take great care that at the beginning of the confession, and especially during its progression, he is not sad, austere, or rigid, especially with those who are timid or simple. For soon the mouth of the sinner will close in fear. But let him be kind and mild, in the manner of a prudent physician, and affable. Therefore, before someone begins to confess who is not accustomed to confessing—much to be presumed of the bashful and the young—he may speak about the ease of confession, and if the situation so demands, ask about his father and mother, so that whoever wishes to confess may take up the boldness to speak; for certain persons out of bashfulness at the beginning lose all memory of what they need to confess, especially young people and women who rarely confess. Then he may proceed to the other instructions that follow. This is shown by Him whose place the confessor, Christ, holds when He says: "They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill" <note>Matthew 9:12</note>. Thus He acted, and did not abhor sinners and publicans in the city, but called them to penance, saying: "The Son of Man is not come to call the just, but sinners" <note>Matthew 9:13</note>. 

Regarding women, he should have this habit: he should not linger long, unless the necessity of the confession demands it. As for those who come frequently, and who wish to confess often, he should restrain them from such excess and from such useless frequency, and a certain time should be assigned to them for confessing, so that he does not hear them outside that time, and he should never expose himself to other frequent conversations. And he should use harsh and rigid words to them rather than soft ones. For, as the venerable Bonaventure says, such women, and those like them, not knowing themselves, even infect the priests incredibly, and without loss of time, they fall into sin by wasting too much time with the priest. Christ taught about the aforementioned rigor of the lips when He said to His most holy Mother: "What is that to me and to thee? My hour is not yet come" <note>John 2:4</note>. Yet, with the aforementioned kindness, He was bountiful to sinners.

<summary>This page outlines the eighth rule for confessors, emphasizing the importance of kindness and affability to encourage the timid, while advising caution and strict time management when dealing with frequent, time-consuming penitents, particularly women.</summary>
<keywords>Confessor, Manuale confessorum, Johannes Nider, penance, pastoral care, bashfulness, moderation</keywords>

Mother and Virgin. The heavens and the earth are full of the majesty of the glory of the fruit of your womb. The glorious choir of the apostles praises you, the mother of their Creator. The white-robed company of blessed martyrs glorifies you, the mother of Christ. The glorious army of confessors calls you the temple of the Trinity. The lovable dance of holy virgins proclaims you the example of virginity and humility. The whole heavenly court honors you as queen. Through the whole world, the Church celebrates you by invoking you. Hope of the Lord of majesty. Venerable and tender mother of the heavenly King. Holy and sweet, pious one, you are the mistress of the angels, you are the gate of paradise. You are the ladder of the heavenly kingdom and of glory, you are the bridal chamber, you are the ark of piety and grace. You are the vein of mercy, you are the spouse and mother of the eternal King. You are the temple and the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, the noble dining-chamber of the whole most blessed Trinity. You are the mediatrix of God and men, the lover of mortals, the illuminator of the heavenly ones. You are the helper of those fighting, the advocate, the compassionate one of the poor, and the refuge of sinners. You are the dispenser of gifts.

I received them unworthily. I exercised them unworthily in sin, and I did not honor persons established in holy orders for the sake of God. I did not perform the penance, fasts, prayers, or alms enjoined upon me for my sins. I neglected to make the profession of my mouth and to receive the communion of the body of Christ. In whatever way I have sinned against the seven sacraments, I state my guilt and render myself culpable to God and to you.

### On the seven theological and cardinal virtues.

Ninth, I sinned by omission, because I neglected to keep the three theological virtues and the four cardinal virtues. In me, there is no true faith in Christ with good works. In me, there is no certain hope for future heavenly goods. In me, there is no charity that loves God above all things, and I have not loved my neighbor as myself. In me, there is no prudence, because I did not perform my actions when and how I ought to have performed them, and I conducted my actions inconsiderately according to the desires of pleasure. In me, there is no fortitude, because I did not manfully subdue interior and exterior passions for Christ, and I did not fear to do base and shameful things. In me, there is no temperance, because I refused to sustain labors, fasts, and tribulations. In me, there is no justice, because I did not turn away from evil, but I neglected to do the good which I was bound to do, and I did not justly give to each one what was his.

### ¶ The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Tenth, I sinned because I did not care for the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. In me, there is no <term>sapientia</term> <gloss>wisdom</gloss> for contemplating divine things. In me, there is no <term>intellectus</term> <gloss>understanding</gloss> for considering the end of my life, the pains of hell, and the day of judgment. In me, there is no <term>consilium</term> <gloss>counsel</gloss> for choosing the good and rejecting the evil. In me, there is no <term>scientia</term> <gloss>knowledge</gloss> for recognizing myself and my deeds. In me, there is no <term>fortitudo</term> <gloss>fortitude</gloss> for resisting temptations, tribulations, and evil thoughts. In me, there is no <term>pietas</term> <gloss>piety</gloss> for having compassion on the poor and the afflicted in heart and deed. In me, there is no <term>timor dei</term> <gloss>fear of God</gloss> for fleeing evil and seeking salvation. In whatever way I have sinned in these, I say my fault.

### ¶ The twelve fruits of the Holy Spirit.

Eleventh, I sinned because I knowingly neglected the twelve fruits of the Holy Spirit. In me, there is no <term>charitas</term> <gloss>charity</gloss>, nor <term>gaudium</term> <gloss>joy</gloss> in the service of God, nor <term>pax</term> <gloss>peace</gloss> with my neighbor, nor <term>patientia</term> <gloss>patience</gloss> in adversities, nor <term>longanimitas</term> <gloss>long-suffering</gloss> amid the follies of others, nor <term>bonitas</term> <gloss>goodness</gloss> in my life, nor <term>benignitas</term> <gloss>kindness</gloss> toward my neighbor, nor <term>modestia</term> <gloss>modesty</gloss>.

He wrote another book on the occasion of the controversies that arose in England between the missionaries of the secular clergy and the religious orders. To settle these, Richard Smith, Bishop of Chalcedon, was sent by Urban VIII; he seemed to favor the religious orders less, and indeed to disturb their ministries rather than promote them. Hence arose complaints and various pamphlets, two of which were accused of criticizing episcopal authority, or certainly of deferring to it too little. Sancyranus seized this opportunity to declaim against the religious orders and published that famous pamphlet on the *Hierarchy* under the assumed name of *Petrus Aurelius*. The work was pleasing as long as the author remained hidden, and it was approved by the Synod of the Gallican Clergy on April 27, 1641, and committed to the press at their expense. Godeau, the Bishop of Grasse, added a eulogy in which the author is heralded as "the most invincible defender of Bishops, the most keen lover of truth, the most just vindicator of the Hierarchy, and a theologian raised in the bosom of ancestral theology." The modesty of Sancyranus did not have enough strength to cause him to prefer remaining hidden any longer amidst such commendation of himself and his labor. But once the author was discovered, a blush covered his face, and all that pomp of words eventually vanished even from the book *Gallia Christiana* <gloss>Christian Gaul</gloss>.

Indeed, he proved himself a candidate of "ancestral theology" in the book condemned on April 23, 1654: *Theologia Familiaris, seu brevis explicatio mysteriorum Fidei* <gloss>Familiar Theology, or a brief explanation of the mysteries of the Faith</gloss>

because of the consistency of the men, who were urged toward subscription by the severe command of the King, the rigid morality of many suffered no small blemish; they signed without setting aside the error in their minds, they committed perjury so that they might be allowed to retain what was theirs or to aspire to new things. Those who were of a more tender conscience, or wished to appear so, looked around for subterfuges and means by which they might mitigate the horror of perjury, and they resorted to equivocations and mental restrictions, which even the most lax morality would shudder at. Thus they condemned the first proposition, and said that grace is given to all the just, by which the commandments of God become possible for them, if they ask for it from God as they ought: but in their minds they retained that the grace of praying as one ought is not given to all the just. They condemned the second, because the small grace of <term>Jansenius</term> <gloss>Cornelius Jansen</gloss>, which excites in us only a weak desire for good, is at the same time inferior to earthly delight (understand this) against which it is not sufficient for victory, and thus it can be resisted: because, they add to themselves, it is always resisted. In the third, they condemned and rejected from their hearts the necessity (suppose) of a natural or physical kind, which makes one act not through choice, but through impulse. Regarding the fourth and fifth, they argued according to the writing of the three columns, and said that without a doubt any preceding grace can be resisted, if the human will should desire, and grace itself (this in silence) would not make it desire. So likewise they conceded that from the merits of the death of Christ certain graces come to the reprobate, but not those without which they could not be saved. Behold the vanity of men!

Yet even this nest was first disturbed by order of the King in the year of Quesnel's <term>Hegira</term> <gloss>flight/exile</gloss>, and the whole congregation was dissolved in 1686, with the author of the book *Innocentia oppressa* <gloss>Oppressed Innocence</gloss> singing their funeral rites at great length.

But these turbulent spirits could not remain hidden for long in Belgium either. They were discovered in the year 1690 by Castanaga, the Governor of Belgium, and ordered to leave Brussels. They complied without delay and went to Leiden in the month of April. However, shortly after, they changed their plan and departed for the territory of Liège, where they settled near a certain castle. Soon considering themselves less safe there, they entered the city itself and kept themselves there until the end of August, known to very few. When they grew weary of being tossed about, they disregarded the danger and furtively returned to Brussels after a space of six months, seeking their old hiding places, from which, according to the testimony of Quesnel himself in certain of his letters, they did not step foot for the entire four years that Arnauld survived. During this time, Quesnel polished his work, and Arnauld, with his assistance, sought to test his final strength against the Bulls of the Popes and against the recent Decree of Alexander VIII, by which 31 propositions and many of Arnauld's were condemned, in the book written as *Difficulties proposed against Steyart, Doctor of Louvain*. Having finished this labor, the elderly man, on the verge of the grave and 82 years of age, received the viaticum from the hands of Quesnel and expired on August 8, 1694.

The anonymous continuator of Briet <note>Philippe Briet, a Jesuit historian</note> in his Appendix adds five full years to his life; from what source, I do not know, and he composes a remarkable eulogy, which it will not be irrelevant to append, illustrated with added notes; it reads as follows.

> In the year 1699, on the 17th day before the Kalends of September <note>August 16</note>, Antonius Arnaldus, a Frenchman and Doctor of the Sorbonne, died in the district of Liège. He was a man regarded by many with ambiguous <note>(a)</note> fame, because he consistently <note>(b)</note> maintained in many writings <note>(c)</note> the efficacy of divine grace <note>(d)</note> of itself against its detractors, with the errors condemned in Corn. Jansenius <note>(e)</note> imputed to him, which he professed to condemn with a sincere judgment together with the Catholic Church until his final breath <note>(f)</note>. He was a man of learning equal to the probity of his character <note>(g)</note>, which he showed by enduring criticism and exile with equal zeal and patience <note>(h)</note>, always with an unconquered and docile spirit <note>(i)</note>. He wrote many books filled with sacred learning <note>(l)</note>, especially in defense of the Most Holy Eucharist, the faith and reverence of which he vigorously defended against the heterodox <note>(m)</note> and the gluttons of the sacred table <note>(n)</note>. Yet he found the minds of some no more appeased toward him <note>(o)</note>; in order to withdraw from their harassment, he turned to a secret solitude, and there he grew old amidst meditations and writing: in the judgment of Innocent XI (hold your laughter), he was at one time to be co-opted among the Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, had not human reason persuaded him (suppress your anger) that this sacrifice should be made for the sake of the Church's peace, to be purchased from his harassers <note>(p)</note>.

These things the anonymous author includes in the Appendix of a Jesuit book—he pursues Nicole, Coddeus the Bishop of Sebaste, and others with a similar eulogy. You will know the bird by its song.

But nothing fair was to be expected from this class of men, who looked to nothing other than securing protection for their work through great names, and preparing by any means a stubborn defense of their errors. The correction could in no way please them: the edition was therefore postponed until the death of Bossuet, after which it appeared immediately in 1699 under the title: *New Testament in French with Moral Reflections on every verse. Paris.* Nothing was deleted in it, nothing corrected; only Bossuet's annotations were prefixed to the work like a shield.

All good men were stunned, until Saint-André, Bossuet's Vicar, who as a witness and arbiter knew everything that had been done by the Bishop in this matter, exposed the most disgraceful frauds. Then indeed the indignation of all erupted, the work was referred to the sacred tribunals, and antidotes against the plague were sought. Meanwhile, Quesnel, having been established as the head of the faction after Arnauld, and Gerberon, having scattered seditious pamphlets throughout Belgium and Gaul as was reported above, taking occasion especially from the aforementioned case of conscience, threw everything into confusion; and by now the unbridled license of those men seemed to be restrainable only by the application of force. But this was the difficult task. Quesnel, by frequently changing his hideouts, his clothing, and his assumed names—now called Father Prior or Provincial of the Augustinians, now Monsieur de Fresne, Frekerberg, Baron de Rebeck, du Puis, etc.—had hitherto eluded the diligence of the most sagacious men.

Finally, Humbert-Guillaume de Precipiano, Archbishop of Mechelen, after he had subjected another priest of the Oratory, Van Hame, to canonical penalties in the year 1700 for spreading principles contrary to the faith despite repeated warnings, and in 1702 had initiated proceedings against Quesnel in Rome, received more certain information regarding their hiding places in the following year. In 1703, he first captured Gerberon, who was dragged from the outermost corner of the city of Brussels. Quesnel himself, along with his inseparable companion Brigode, who—although warned by Roman letters to depart the city—had only changed his lodgings by moving to the house called *Refuge de Forest* <gloss>Refuge of the Forest</gloss>, was discovered there. With the help of his companion, Quesnel had already escaped the hands of the approaching officers, but, recalled by the memory of papers which were of the greatest importance to hide from the eyes of men, he was intercepted by hidden guards in the month of May, and on the Wednesday after Pentecost, he was likewise taken to the Prelate's Palace.

Quesnel remained there for no more than three months. For his associates, having explored every crack to find a way to offer help, finally used a note, drawn through the windows by a lead weight and addressed to Ernest, a Canon of Saint Gudula, to inform him of the place, location, and condition of his confinement. They perforated the wall with labor continued over two nights, and thus, on September 13th after midnight, they restored their precious leader to liberty, who soon fled into Holland. All of his papers that were intercepted showed what he had prepared to disturb the peace of the Church. Among other things, a voluminous work was discovered: *Dogmata, disciplina, & doctrina moralis Ecclesiæ* <gloss>Dogmas, Discipline, and Moral Doctrine of the Church</gloss>, in which the Eccle-

With this understood, Noailles, without delay, issued a mandate on the 28th of the same month, in which he stated that he could no longer permit his name to be attached to a book condemned by the Pope. Consequently, as he had promised, he revoked the approval he had previously given in another diocese to a book already approved by his predecessor, condemned the book, and prohibited its reading and retention. The clergy were then convoked, and commissioners were elected, the leader of whom was Cardinal Rohan; Noailles was named president of the council. They met on October 18th. Out of 18 Archbishops, seven were present; out of 112 Bishops, thirty-three. Noailles began by speaking of the preface he had once given to the book and of the mandate he had published shortly before. He soon began to lecture on the obscurity of the Bull and the doubts that would arise from it, to the astonishment of the others, to whom everything in it seemed clear and plain. Rohan demonstrated that there was not one of the 101 propositions to which one of the censures did not apply. Noailles, however, contended as much as he could that the Bull could not be accepted otherwise than with a prefixed instruction and the addition of certain explanations and restrictions. This proposal was rejected by almost everyone, and Cardinal Rohan opposed it with four articles: 1. It is manifest from the Bull and must be maintained that the book of Quesnel is heretical; 2. Those 101 propositions are deservedly condemned and worthy of one of the stated censures; 3. Therefore, the Bull must be accepted before any further explanation, as it is neither ambiguous nor obscure regarding the aforementioned points; 4. No other prior instruction is needed, except one to safeguard the faithful against false interpretations of the Bull. These points pleased the assembly, but not Noailles, who, when nothing

All of these things were approved by the Pontiff. And when the responses of most of the absent Bishops had arrived, by which they also approved the acts and signified their acceptance of the Bull by their given consent, the King on February 14th issued an edict, or letters patent, by which he commanded the Bull to be accepted, published, and observed by all, and to be entered into the public records by all Parliaments throughout the Kingdom. Soon the Bull was promulgated in 113 dioceses. Compliance was also given by the Parliaments, but not entirely well; for although the Bishops publicly protested that the Gallican liberties <note>original: "libertatibus gallicanis"; the traditional independence of the French Church from absolute papal authority</note> were in no way derogated by the Bull, nevertheless, formulas of caution were added by them, omitting the protests of the Bishops, which would cause new disturbances in their own time.

The King inhibited the decision of the Parliament and summoned the case to the Aulic Council <note>the King's Privy Council</note>. From this, the decrees of the Congregation were approved and confirmed by Royal authority. Upon understanding this, twenty-six abandoned their cells and, having shed their religious habit, fled into Holland. Shortly after, fifteen others from the Abbey of Orval followed them to Utrecht <note>original: "Ultrajectum"</note>, led by the Abbot himself and the Master of Novices. Many others, indeed, of various status and condition, both from Paris and Nantes, and among these the most conspicuous ornament of the faction, a Deacon of Paris, in the following year, 1726, openly sought the communion of the schismatic Archbishop of Utrecht.

Noailles was still more terrified by the Council of Embrun <note>original: "Concilium Ebredunense"</note> and by the King's authority in defending its acts. In the year 1727, many bishops had gathered at Embrun to overthrow the immense errors that were being scattered everywhere by the schismatics, and to compose the disturbances incited by them. Furthermore, there were two principal acts: the condemnation of Father Courrayer <note>original: "P. Courrayer"</note> from the monastery of Saint Genevieve <note>original: "S. Genovefæ"</note> along with his book against the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, who, intending to carry out the system of Dupin <note>original: "Dupini"</note>, crossed over into England and exalted himself there with other writings concerning the ordinations of Anglican bishops; the other act was the sentence passed on the 20th of September against Soanen, the Bishop of Senez <note>original: "Suanenium Senetiensem"</note>. Under his name, a certain pastoral Instruction had appeared, teeming with shameful errors of every kind, and by which, as much as the work of Quesnel <note>original: "Quesnelli"</note> was commended, so much was the Bull condemning it held up as if it were worthy of every execration. Soanen, having initially prevaricated, and with thirteen Bishops having been named before whom he might plead his cause, and against whom he himself had no objections, finally set out for Embrun <note>original: "Ebredunum"</note>, not without a profane escort, and one that was not unarmed. But before he entered the city, he ordered it to be announced to those who had gathered that he would never recognize them as judges. Subsequently, when asked by the Council whether that Instruction was his, he indeed denied that it had been composed by him, yet nonetheless openly professed that he entirely adopted, held, and approved it as his own until he could be convinced of the errors which the Bishops had condemned within it. Indeed, the obstinacy of this man could not be overcome. Therefore, by the sentence of the Council, he was interdicted from every function, both Episcopal and Priestly, and a Vicar General was appointed for his diocese. It would be a long task to recount the clamors and tumults which this scene provoked. Twelve Bishops protested against this sentence and brought their protestation to the King himself. Fifty advocates of the Parisian Court signed a consultation regarding the nullity of the sentence and the acts of the Council of Embrun. The clergy of Senez, supported by a mob of monks and others, rejected the Vicar appointed by the Council and refused to obey anyone other than Soanen’s previous Vicar, named la Porte. But the Protestation of the Bishops was rejected by the King, the Consultation of the Advocates was suppressed by his authority, the clamors of the others were repressed by command, the Vicar la Porte was arrested, and thus quiet was restored to the entire Province; the Constitution was promulgated throughout the entire diocese and was accepted by all, with few

And with this, all the plans the Duke had conceived in his mind to lead the Cardinal back to the right path were finally overturned.

Meanwhile, the Appellants triumphed, though not without grief for the death of Quesnel, their leader—most esteemed after Arnauld—from whom this whole present cause was derived. It is not my intention here to weave the history of this man's life; it is useful to add only two things to what has already been said about him that are worthy of memory. The first is a certain writing sent by Quesnel himself to a certain Priest, who, having finally wiped away the darkness of errors, was returned to himself and the Church and revealed it. The rules were comprised in 12 articles, which his followers were to use in conversation among themselves and with various kinds of people. The summary was nearly this: Union and concord: fidelity to the secret: circumspection in speech according to the varying condition of men: ambiguity <note>original: "amphibologia"</note> in various heads of Religion: he wished it to be said that they hold Christ present in the Eucharist, not merely by faith or figure, as the heterodox do, but neither by transubstantiation, nor substantially, nor really, as Catholics say; how then? in an imperceptible manner. In the Sacrament of Penance, they were to urge the insufficiency of attrition and the necessity of perfect contrition. That they should openly impugn sufficient grace, the liberty of indifference, and merits, and at other times do so through the vagueness of words, so that an escape might be open to those hard-pressed: that they should uniquely extol victorious grace: and so many other things. Quesnel, when asked by his nephew Pinfon, a sculptor, to which party in the then-litigating matters of Religion he ought to accede, replied by letter: "He should hold himself on the side of the greater number of the faithful, or firmly adhere to the trunk of the tree of the Church; for he himself had been provoked and compelled to foster these litigations so pertinaciously only by the injuries of the Jesuits." Pinfon asserted that he had heard this same thing in person, and not just once, from the mouth of Quesnel himself, as attested by the Bishop of Angers, Poncet de la Rivière, in his *Reflexiones consolatoriæ* <gloss>Consolatory Reflections</gloss>. But from the time that fury seized the man, in the year 1719 at Amsterdam, having been led to the borders of death in extreme old age, four days before his passing he renewed his appeal, and having thus received Viaticum <gloss>the Eucharist administered to the dying</gloss> from his Pastor, the old man lived until the 2nd of December, at the age of 85.

Furthermore, the fruits of those disturbances were most tragic indeed. To say nothing of the countless writings of fanatical men, by which they labored to destroy human and divine laws, let one or two facts suffice to understand the nature of the heresy. Dupin, a Doctor of the Sorbonne, held frequent correspondence with the Archbishop of Canterbury, which was at first believed to have been begun and continued for the sake of learning and courtesy, but eventually became suspect. Therefore, when Dupin's papers were suddenly seized, it was revealed that he had been plotting nothing less than to betray the Catholic Religion and to attempt to reconcile the union and communion of the Gallican Church with the Anglican. to us pastors, he attempts to tear asunder those who are most closely joined as members of the same body, so that, just as he has sown those disastrous discords in the middle of Germany, he might also disseminate the same dissensions in the Gallic Churches on account of <term>Ubiquity</term> <gloss>the doctrine that Christ's human body is omnipresent</gloss>. Now Osiander is, so that you might know the man, a <term>diapyros</term> <gloss>a firebrand/incendiary</gloss> and carrier of a new kind of Pandora, forged by some Vulcan or other, which he has undertaken to transport to other regions and provinces of the world as well, such as to Gaul and Belgium. But he either considers you to be blocks and stocks, who would for so long tolerate such bitter things for a doctrine unknown to you and not at all weighed according to the standard of the Divine word, as if it were a just balance: or, if he deems you pious and prudent, he certainly should have thought well of you, and believed that you have done carefully what is written <margin>Acts 17. The fifth mode of discernment is if there is weight of humility in the deeds, words, gestures, and morals of that spirit, just as weight is usually grasped in a coin. For example, if the weeping, groaning, complaint, petition, recognition of sins, or confession of guilt or of pains is heard from it, or similar things, such that there is no glorification, boasting, domination, blasphemy, or disparagement or cursing. I am now writing to inform you of the order in which these matters were managed by me. As soon as I arrived in the province, I immediately asked the people of that region whether a merchant fleet was still free to depart. Having been sufficiently instructed by them on this matter, I betook myself to <term>Alexandria</term> <gloss>a major port city in Egypt</gloss>. I expedited your first shipments and took care of all matters concerning my own affairs that I knew of, so that I would not let the time—which was quite brief for the rest of your business—pass in idleness. I gathered cargo from all sides and brought into the harbor those ships that were most prepared for sailing. By the ides of March, when everything had already been placed on board, the sailors departed from the port; and as the winds were favorable, almost all of them raised their sails at the same time. What followed from this was reported to me not long after. Scarcely two or three ships at most reached the shore, if any of those were yours. The others, it is said, suffered shipwreck. I hear that, because of the fear of the storm, they have not yet moved from that port, but that they will make the journey to us as soon as that storm has subsided. May our news turn out well. I wished these things to be known to you first by our triremes, so that you might be better informed about all your affairs and lay aside any anxiety you might perhaps have conceived from this shipwreck. In other matters, since you are a prudent man, there is nothing about which I need to admonish you. For you can sufficiently judge for yourself that the merchandise is much more valuable, even had there been no shipwreck. I shall expedite the rest when the time comes. If you wish me to do anything else regarding your affairs, signify it to me through your letters. Farewell.

So that for the salvation of good men, and for the sake of friends, we may not be broken by any troubles. Let us show ourselves <note>original: "placabiles"</note> accommodating not only to those whom we ought to love and protect, but even <note>original: "exorabiles"</note> yielding to our enemies. If you remember what each one of us owes to duty, I will congratulate you; and I will congratulate myself greatly if I understand that my letters have added anything to your talent and virtue, so that you may achieve more quickly all those things which you see are sought by you with great study, and with no less progress. Farewell.</meta>

<note>A red decorative initial N marks the beginning of the letter.</note>

Not that I would consider that I had done enough for the Republic <note>original: "reipublicae"</note> and for my friends, if I had not expected you to admonish me in that matter which, while honest with others, would also be necessary for me. But since I have refrained from public affairs because of my age, and have never fled from any labors or dangers for its sake, I seemed to myself to have retreated, as if into a port of my life, without injury to my country. And this was also to be granted by all citizens and by my own kin, so that I, who had sailed on the sea for a long time, might finally moor myself in the port. But it is as it is in other things: there is in friendship and love for one’s country a certain excessive desire and longing in men, which can never be satisfied. I do not know what more either my country or my friends want from me, or why I should again renew the troubles of old age, and, while I can still live for myself for some time, seem to have thrust my hands into the fire. Do not—if you love me—urge me toward that matter which befits neither this age nor my studies. Our Republic already has enough protection, if it uses the counsels of those citizens whom it holds. For me, however, rest should have been earned by my merits in public service. You, however, if you defend the cause of your friend before the citizens, I hold greater thanks for this than if you were to praise my leisure.

<summary>The author explains his retirement from public life as a well-earned rest after years of service, politely resisting calls to return to active politics despite the insistence of his friends.</summary>
<keywords>Gasparino, Republic, res publica, retirement, duty, civic service, friendship</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: ...if I did not know</meta> how it happens that my thoughts see me as more dull with him <note>referring to the friend</note> whom we love, even when we are absent from them, and we think about their pursuits, conversations, or counsels for us within ourselves. I think this happens to us because our affection has something greater and more noble than our senses can reach. It dwells, indeed, in the soul, where they are also stored. Therefore, the matter would be very pleasing to me if, whenever you have someone to whom you can entrust your letters, you would write something to me. For I seem to be with you whenever I read your letters. Nor let our friendship be idle; if anything happens in which your work can be of use to me, or mine to you, let it be so. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' is present.</note>

No one in these days do I think lives who is more unfortunate than I. For such discomfort surrounds me that I see no exit for myself, unless that which delay might bring me. I am now so miserable that I am everywhere exposed to fortune, wherever she might strike me. I have lost my country, in which I flourished for a long time with honor and dignity. As for my paternal goods, it has been said to me <note>that they are gone</note>. The associates I had in the republic, the violence of civil wars has taken away. All who were friends have either perished or are with me in the same calamity. What more remains for me, wretched man, than to put an end to such evils by death? Believe me, I am not only lacking counsel, but I even seem to myself to have become mad. I used to relieve my sorrow of soul by reading or writing, but now there are no arts at all that delight me. I desire your presence greatly. I hope that, either by grieving with me or by consoling me, you will bring some solace to me in such great sadness. It could not be that (with the prudence and wisdom you have always had) you might not have some counsel for me so that I might bear all things less bitterly. Since you can do this, strive to come here, or if occupations detain you, <unclear>something</unclear>

How much your letter has afflicted me with grief, to such an extent that I myself stand in need of great consolation. Just as our sense of things previously found pleasure in light matters, so now that those things have been disturbed and cast down, by which you long flourished among your fellow citizens, I am moved by no less a disturbance of spirit, as if everything had befallen my own affairs. For what can be called more mine than that which is yours? You have me more as a companion and participant in your hardships than as a consoler. But where there is such a power and magnitude of genius, as to be able to console yourself through letters and through my presence, you have certainly, at one and the same time, brought some aid to both of us. But I am not sufficiently capable on my own, nor have I ever been a suitable teacher for this matter. What I can easily do, that I will perform. In the first days, I will come to you, and if grief is lightened by grieving <note>an allusion to the custom of sharing sorrows to diminish them</note> (whatever kind of consolation that may be), I will not omit anything in diminishing your grief. Meanwhile, you will borrow some counsel from letters and from philosophy, and you will be mindful that you are the same person. For since you are held to be the wisest of almost all men who live in this our age, consider how it conforms to the expectation of those to whom you are known, that you should be conquered by grief, you who have always borne prosperous Fortune with restraint. I do not write this on my own account, but since the eyes of many are cast upon you, I often hear men’s conversation held about you. I, however, respond to that by saying that it is impossible for you not to feel such a great calamity and loss of things, but yet that you bear all things with an even mind, according to your wisdom. Nor do I think that counsel or a remedy is lacking to you, by which you may cure this sickness. You will therefore do what I most desire in this your grief. You will stand with a raised spirit, and by enduring, you will conquer fortune, which previously conquered you. If you do this, you will certainly gain greater glory from your victory than from all <unclear>other things</unclear>

<summary>This page contains a letter of consolation addressed to a friend suffering from political and personal misfortune, urging him to maintain his stoic reputation and use philosophy to endure his current distress.</summary>
<keywords>consolation, philosophy, fortune, friendship, stoicism, wisdom, adversity</keywords>

<note>A decorative red initial 'L' introduces the text.</note> I have recently read the letters sent to me by you, from which I have indeed received great perturbation. But I am angry with you, because you wrote to me so late regarding your extreme poverty. For I judge that if this had been written to me in time, I would have dedicated effort to our friends so that your poverty would not have been so grievous and troublesome. <note>A decorative red paragraph mark appears here.</note> (As I see, and as you write to me) shame was an impediment to you, and it is a vice of all nobility, which considers it no less shameful to beg for assistance from another in near-destitution than to be in need. You will blame yourself if, with friends unaware, you have been tormented by this trouble for longer than was necessary. What is pressing, I will take care of, so that in the future you will not be in these inconveniences in which you have been until now, and therefore [you must] proceed with such modesty that neither excessive shame is incurred for you, nor negligence for your friends. I am sending you a small amount of money, until better provision can be made by me and our friends. I beg you, do not despair of your friends. I (to speak of myself) will see to it that in no way (with my abundance) will I allow you to labor under any lack of material things. I judge that all those who loved you for your own sake should know this. Farewell.

<note>A decorative red initial 'A' introduces the text.</note> For my grandfather (which I see happens to many) to have been reduced to poverty, I bear it in my mind with my fortune somewhat aggrieved. But since all my studies, through which I have done well by many, have fallen into nothing, I cannot be sufficiently acquiescent. How could I bring myself to be treated badly by those for whom I have always been frugal and liberal? You know well enough the favors and services which our citizens have extracted from me. But how ungrateful they were toward me, the time itself has taught. For when those men, whom I had made my friends for the sake of the common salvation, had breathed against me, and had suborned judges, and had instructed false witnesses against me, who defended my right regarding my own? Or who wished to protect my dignity? But I feel that it happens deservedly that I experience those to be ungrateful, in whom
