X.text:
<meta>continues from previous page: ...diligently, and that there was no calculation regarding me, I know well, and I understand this to be a true maxim: that in an old proverb, all those who fall into a snare because of others, excuse themselves at their own risk. But if the matter could return to its previous state, I would certainly regret it this time. Meanwhile, I am penalized by the pain. It is of no consequence to them. I wrote this to you, not because I expect your advice or protection in a desperate situation, but because I feel my pain is relieved when I speak to you about my inconveniences. Farewell.</meta>

<note>A large red decorative initial 'N' appears here.</note>
It is not a new matter that you write to me, nor is it unknown to me. For how often have you believed that I, by the indignity of such fortune, have frequently and properly endured this from other citizens and those I considered outstanding, despite my own goodness and fairness? Although this calamity of ours is of no consequence to yours, yet it happens (I know not how) that we suffer less from evils that are common in the city. However, I would prefer that you borrow aid for this perturbation from your own wisdom rather than from common custom. For I know this will be the result, that nothing will relieve your distress more than the fact that none of these things has happened to you because of your own merit. And the opinion you hold of your situation will change if you consider your greater losses, rather than the perturbation which is still fresh. But you write to me in this desperate matter, not for the sake of protection or advice, but because it helps you to speak to me about your inconveniences. You do what is customary among friends. I am accustomed to doing the same. Knowing that I am relieved in spirit, I seem to myself to have laid aside the greater part of my troubles when I have laid bare all my perturbation to my friends. I rejoice greatly in this, and I give you thanks that you have chosen me from among many to whom you might entrust your cares. By these and other signs, and also by this one, I judge that I am greatly loved by you. As for the rest, which pertains to your consolation, you yourself will better foresee it (as I hope) by your own wisdom than by my letters. Farewell.

<summary>Gasparino continues his correspondence by acknowledging a friend's distress, offering empathy through shared experience, and encouraging his friend to rely on personal wisdom rather than common customs to manage misfortune.</summary>
<keywords>Gasparino, Epistolae, consolation, friendship, distress, wisdom, correspondence</keywords>

If a religious puts aside the habit for a shameful cause, as if going by night to a brothel, he incurs it; but it is different if he does not put aside the habit, but hides it inside or covers it with another so that he is not recognized, especially if he does it for a good cause, for example, because it is hot and he does not want his religion to be recognized, provided he is still wearing the religious habit. But he who puts it aside for fear of robbers does not put it aside rashly. Nor are those excused who change their habit in schools so that they do not appear as religious. But he who puts it aside out of playful levity for an hour so that he may run or throw a stone does not incur it, because it is credible that he intended to avoid the fault in all minor things, to avoid falling into such snares. ¶ <term>Second</term> is against religious who go to the studies of the friars, unless license has been granted with the counsel of their convent or the greater part of it, with the license to go to study <note>original: "concessa"</note>. Regarding such persons, however, who had received something as a gift and had consumed it before they understood the truth of the matter, they are not held to restore it. 
Similarly, an exception is made when someone acts in the case of those spoiled of their goods by warning and inducing, as much as they can, the <term>raptor</term> <gloss>robber</gloss> himself to make restitution, especially if there is a probable hope for the correction of the plunderers, and when he becomes powerless to make restitution in whole or in large part through such a person’s consumption. Those admonishers, therefore, who insist at opportune hours so that the plunderer may restore the stolen goods, are not held to make restitution. Under the second case, likewise, those who know or probably believe that, because of their own following or association with the robbers or other incitement or detraction, the robbers themselves did not do more than they would have done otherwise, and yet they received some of the stolen goods and spent them, such persons are held to restore from the goods held or spent, and also for all the <term>dampnum</term> <gloss>damage</gloss> that they or any of their family caused directly or occasionally. 
Third, when several persons together cause damage, and just as one would have done it without the other, or several without this one, such a person is held to pay <term>pro rata</term> <gloss>in proportion</gloss>, that is, for his own share, which is as much as takes away from the total damage if it is not possible to distinguish the damage that he himself brought about from that which others brought about. In this judgment, however, it should be held that he who is more vigorous and who inflicted greater fear and terror on the victims is also held to more. Likewise, in the case when some associate with robbers and believe that even without their own assistance or instigation the robbers would have caused the damage, they are only held for that which they probably believe the robbers caused through their own instigation or assistance. 
Fourth, if some associate with the robbers and do not cooperate with them in causing any damage, but are nonetheless in their minds prepared to defend them if, perchance, those being despoiled had wished to defend their goods from the robbers, and because of their presence and that of their associates, they [the victims] did not dare to resist those despoiling them.

Indeed, if some people go with robbers with the intention of keeping the peace, they are not excused unless they signal this to the adversaries, because otherwise the adversaries would not dare to defend their own property due to fear of them. Hence, it is as if they helped them. If they have encouraged the adversaries, which then appears to be the first case, he who was the cause of all the damage is held <term>in solidum</term> <gloss>as a whole/jointly and severally</gloss>, that is, for the entire damage. This is the case where there were many robbers, none of whom induced another to come, nor did any lord <note>or master</note> command another, but each says for himself: "If we go, it is as if we were an army." Each is held <term>in solidum</term> <gloss>as a whole</gloss>, because in such a case each helped the others and made them stronger, and all are <term>cooperatores</term> <gloss>co-operators</gloss>. Otherwise, if they did not go together but each was making the damage separately by himself, each is held for that which he did. Understand this beyond what has already been said, because one would not dare or be able to cause the damage without the other. Otherwise, everyone is held for the part of the damage that they incurred. Note also that stolen or plundered property must be restored with all the fruits and profits that it yielded, or that could have been yielded, because they are held to <term>interesse</term> <gloss>damages/compensation</gloss> and to all losses. Nor is one excused if the item perishes while in their possession, because they were in delay of restitution. If, however, the owner was offered it and refused to accept, they are excused. Furthermore, regarding any damage where restitution must be made because the one causing damage did so unjustly, they are not only held to restore the item, but also to <term>interesse</term>, that is, to the making good of the loss, and to the fruit perceived from the item if the item was fruitful. However, they are not held to the fruit that comes from the industry of the one using that item. <note>A red paragraph mark begins the sixth and seventh rules.</note>

The sixth rule: let the confessor, about to hear women, take care that while he purges their souls from vices, he himself does not become defiled by voluntary pleasures. Let him not be like a cloth that becomes dirty while washing others, but rather like a hand that becomes clean while cleaning others. Therefore, let him not believe himself a respecter of persons when he listens to beautiful or young women more freely and easily than old women in confession. Let him protect himself with good and holy imaginations. First, by considering that he ought to be an angel of God and a vicar of God trembling at the judgment. Then, when the eyes of his body turn from a verse or a passage to the women, let him see with the eyes of his soul that they are like an image of God that is leprous or wounded by the dire demons of mortal sins, or at least wrinkled or scabrous with venial faults, which must be healed through the blood of Christ and the sacrament of penance. Let the confessor secretly press his thumb with the sign of the cross for his own sake to protect his purity. Let him invoke God with at least a brief prayer, and let him avoid, without necessity, sweet words and any useless chatter. And thus, let him apply himself solely to the honor of God and the salvation of another's soul. Nor should he despair if he is tempted while he resists the pleasure of the flesh, mindful of where Christ says to the disciples: If they drink any deadly thing, it will not hurt them. He removes the appearance of evil, etc. Regarding which the blessed Gregory says: Priests, by their good exhortations, remove malice from the hearts of others, they remove the appearance of evil, and while they hear of pestilential temptations and are not led to wicked thoughts by them, it is a deadly thing that they drink and it will not hurt them. The same is advised in his Pastoral Care, where he says: It happens often that while the soul of the rector knows the temptations of another, he is also struck by hearing those temptations, and those things are by no means to be feared by the shepherd, because he easily rescues his own soul from them and also, through mercy, he is fatigued by the temptation of another. Saint Thomas confirms this in the fourth [book of the Sentences], saying that the prayer which one gives in the sacrament of penance restores, if any inclination to sin arises from the circumstance of the thought, namely of carnal things necessarily spoken, either in the one confessing or in the confessor.

The seventh rule: the confessor should not look at the face of the one confessing, especially if it is a woman, lest she blush and lest he be wounded in his soul by the woman, as if by a spiritual surgeon.

as, according to that of Habakkuk: He will make his wind to blow <note>referring to the breath of temptation</note>. Whence the gloss upon that in Genesis: She saw that the tree was delectable to the sight. Say: Lest we slip in our thoughts, we ought not to gaze upon what it is not lawful to desire. For just as a pure mind in its thought is accustomed to be filled by the lascivious delight of its own, so are the eyes, like certain robbers, of guilt. For Eve would not have touched the tree if she had not first looked upon it imprudently. It must be pondered how much we ought to restrain ourselves from illicit things, because we live in a state of mortality, if one who is living comes to death through the eyes.

The eighth rule: The confessor must take great care that at the beginning of the confession, and especially in the course of it, he is not sad, austere, or rigid, particularly to those who are shy, fearful, or simple. For soon he will close the mouth of the sinner. Rather, he should be kind and mild, in the manner of a prudent physician, and affable. Therefore, before anyone begins to confess who is not accustomed to confessing—greatly consider the shy and the young—he may say things pertaining to confession, and if the situation demands it, ask about his or her status. Let everyone who wishes to confess take the courage to speak, because certain persons, out of shyness, lose all memory of what they need to confess at the beginning, especially the young and women who confess rarely. Then let him proceed to the other teachings that follow. This is shown by Him whose place the confessor, Christ, takes when He says: They that are whole need not the physician, but they that are sick. Thus, the same One acted, who did not abhor sinners in the city and the tax collectors, but called them to penance, saying: The Son of Man did not come to call the just, but sinners.

Regarding women, he should have a habit of not delaying too long, unless the necessity of the confession demands it. Those who are truly repentant and who wish to confess frequently should be warned against such excess and against such useless frequency. Let a fixed time be assigned to them for confessing, lest at that time he hear them, nor should he ever expose himself to other frequent conversations. And he should use harder and more rigid words to them than soft ones, because, as the venerable Bonaventure says, such women, and those like them, not knowing themselves and the priests, infect them incredibly; without the loss of time that they incur while they sin, they waste too much time. Christ taught us about the aforementioned rigor toward one’s own when He said to His most holy Mother: What is it to me and to thee? My hour has not yet come. Nevertheless, through the aforementioned kindness toward sinners...

In me there is no fortitude <note>original: "fortitudo"</note> for resisting temptations, tribulations, and evil thoughts. In me there is no piety <note>original: "pietas"</note> for sympathizing with the poor and the afflicted in heart and deed. In me there is no fear of God <note>original: "timor dei"</note> for fleeing evil and seeking salvation. In whatever way I have sinned in these, I state my guilt.

X.text:
<note>A decorative red initial 'R' at the beginning of the text.</note>Remember, Lord Jesus, that it is not Yours to lose anything of that which Your Father has given to You, but it is Yours specifically to have mercy always and to spare. To lose no one, but to save, because Your Father sent You into the world, not that You might judge the world, but that we might have life through You, so that You might be for us and not against us. For You paid what we owed, You atoned for what we sinned, and You supplied what we neglected. May Your bitter death, therefore, and the price of Your shed blood, and the renewal of Your satisfaction, and the venerable mystery of Your body and blood, which is offered to You daily in the Church for the salvation of the faithful, provide for me now and at my end a plenary, nay, an overflowing satisfaction. In this, You are the priest and the sacrifice: the one who offers, the one to whom it is offered, and that which is offered. May it serve to earn in the present the grace which I have not merited, and to obtain in the future the rest and glory which Your pious passion has gained. Your eyes, Lord, saw my imperfection, but do not, O pious God, count it against me for eternal punishment, You who have ordained all things for the highest and perfect good, most excellently and most perfectly. And do not permit me to be erased from the book of life, but offer to me the portion that falls to me in the aid of Your precious passion, with which You willed to make man a co-heir to You in the land of the living. let the world cry out, for the world remains the world and does not change. Let God do what He will, the Devil does not cease his work in his instruments. Nevertheless, it must be said to the godless world so that it has no excuse today, or tomorrow, or on the Day of Judgment, as if it had known nothing of it or had not been warned, just as the prophet is commanded there: Cry aloud, spare not, lift up your voice like a trumpet, and show my people their transgression, whether they wish to repent and live. If they do not wish to, then you have done your part and saved your soul, but their sin will come upon their own head. Some clergy themselves agree with the godless mob, who indeed bear the name of clergy but are in fact spiritless, and reveal by their fruits what spirit's children they are, for every tree is known by its fruits. However, one dare not murmur, or one has them at one's throat: Do you wish to revile the preaching office? You are then a <term>Weigelianer</term> <gloss>follower of Valentin Weigel</gloss>. He wrote another book on the occasion of the controversies that arose in England between missionaries from the secular clergy and the regular clergy. To resolve these, Richard Smith, Bishop of Chalcedon, was sent by Urban VIII. He appeared to favor the regulars less and, indeed, rather to disturb than to promote their ministries. Hence there were complaints and various pamphlets, two of which were accused of attacking episcopal authority, or at least of showing it too little respect. Sancyranus seized upon this occasion to declaim against the regulars and issued that famous booklet concerning the *Hierarchy* <note>original: "Hierarchia"</note> under the pseudonym of *Petrus Aurelius*. The work was well-received as long as the author remained hidden, and it was approved by the Synod of the Gallican Clergy on April 27, 1641, and committed to the press at their expense. Godeau, Bishop of Grasse, added a eulogy in which the author is proclaimed as "the most invincible defender of Bishops, the most keen lover of truth, the most just vindicator of the Hierarchy, a Theologian raised in the bosom of ancestral Theology." The modesty of Sancyranus did not have enough strength to allow him to remain hidden longer in the face of such praise for himself and his labor. But once the author was discovered, a blush covered his face, and all that pomp of words eventually vanished even from the book *Gallia Christiana* <gloss>Christian Gaul</gloss>.

Indeed, he proved himself a candidate of ancestral Theology in the book condemned on April 23, 1654: *Theologia Familiaris, seu brevis explicatio mysteriorum Fidei* <gloss>Familiar Theology, or a brief explanation of the mysteries of the Faith</gloss>

They subscribed without abandoning the error in their hearts; they perjured themselves so that they might be allowed to retain their own possessions or aspire to new ones. Thus, they condemned the first proposition and said that grace is given to all the just, by which the commandments of God become possible for them if they seek it from God as they ought: but in their hearts, they maintained that the grace to pray as one ought is not given to all the just. They condemned the second, because Jansenius’s "small grace," which excites in us only a weak desire for the good, is simultaneously inferior to earthly pleasure—understand this—which is not sufficient for it to be overcome; therefore, it can be resisted because, they add among themselves, it is always resisted. In the third, they condemned and rejected from their hearts a necessity—suppose a natural or physical one—which causes one to act not by choice, but by impulse. Regarding the fourth and fifth, they discoursed according to the writing of the three columns, and said that, without doubt, any preventing grace can be resisted if the human will should wish it, and grace itself—this they kept silent—would not make it wish it. Likewise, they conceded that certain graces come to the reprobate from the merits of Christ’s death, but not those without which they could not be saved. Behold the vanity of men!

All good men were stunned, until Saint-André, the Vicar of Bossuet, who as a witness and arbiter knew all that had been done by the Bishop in this affair, exposed the most shameful frauds. Then, indeed, the indignation of all erupted; the work was reported to the sacred tribunals, and antidotes were sought against the plague. Meanwhile, Quesnel, having been established as the head of the faction after Arnauld, and Gerberon, with seditious pamphlets scattered throughout Belgium and Gaul, as was related above, having taken the opportunity especially from the aforementioned case of conscience, threw everything into confusion; and by now the unbridled license of those men seemed to be restrained only by the application of force. Finally, Humbert-Guillaume de Precipiano, Archbishop of Mechelen, after subjecting another priest of the Oratory, Van Hame, to canonical penalties in the year 1700 for spreading heterodox principles despite repeated warnings, and after initiating legal action against Quesnel in Rome in 1702, at last seized Gerberon in Brussels in 1703, extracting him from a remote corner of the city after receiving more reliable intelligence concerning his hideouts the previous year. Quesnel himself was later apprehended in the same manner, along with his constant companion Brigode, who, despite having been warned by Roman authorities to leave the city, had merely changed lodgings and moved into the house called *Refuge de Forest*. With the help of his associate, he had already evaded the grasp of the pursuing officers, but was recalled by his hidden keepers due to the importance of the papers he had been keeping from the eyes of men. He was intercepted in the month of May and, on the Wednesday after Pentecost, was likewise brought into the Bishop's Palace.

Quesnel remained there for no more than three months. His partisans, exploring every crevice to find a way to offer him assistance, finally sent a note to Ernest, Canon of Saint Gudula, the location, situation, and condition of his confinement having been conveyed by lowering the message on a lead weight from the windows. Through two nights of continuous work, they bored through the wall, and thus, on September 13th after midnight, they restored their precious leader to liberty, and he soon fled to Holland. All of his intercepted papers showed what he had been preparing to disturb the peace of the Church. And with these, finally, all the plans the Duke had conceived in his mind to bring the Cardinal back to the path were overturned.

Meanwhile, the Appellants triumphed, though not without grief for the death of Quesnel, their leader most esteemed after Arnauld, from whom this whole present cause is derived. It is not my intention to weave here the history of this man's life; it is helpful to add only two things worthy of memory to what has already been said about him. The first is a certain writing sent by Quesnel himself to a certain Priest, who, having at last wiped away the darkness of his errors and returned to himself and to the Church, produced it. These were rules comprised in 12 articles, which his followers were to use in conversation among themselves and with various kinds of men. The gist of it was almost this: Union and concord: loyalty to the secret: circumspection in speech according to the varying condition of men: ambiguity <note>original: "amphibologia"</note> regarding various heads of Religion: he wished it to be said that they consider Christ present in the Eucharist, not merely by faith or figure, as the heterodox do, but neither by <term>transubstantiatio</term> <gloss>transubstantiation</gloss>, nor substantially, nor really, as Catholics say; how then? The decrees of the Congregation were approved by this body and confirmed by royal authority. Upon learning this, twenty-six left their cells, shed their religious habit, and fled to Holland. Shortly thereafter, fifteen others from the Abbey of Orval followed them to Utrecht, led by the Abbot himself and the Master of Novices. Many others of various status and condition, both Parisians and from Nantes—and among them the most conspicuous ornament of the faction, a Deacon of Paris in the following year, 1726—openly sought the communion of the schismatic Archbishop of Utrecht.

Noailles was terrified even more by the Council of Embrun and by the King's authority in defending its acts. In the year 1727, many Bishops had gathered at Embrun to overthrow the massive errors that were being scattered everywhere by the schismatics and to settle the disturbances stirred up by them. Two main acts were carried out. The first was the condemnation of Father Courrayer of the monastery of Saint Geneviève, along with his book against the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist. He had traveled to England to execute the system of Dupin <note>Louis Ellies du Pin, a French ecclesiastical historian</note>, and distinguished himself there with other writings on the ordinations of Anglican Bishops. The second act was the sentence passed on the 20th of September against the Bishop of Senez, Soanen. Fifty advocates of the Parisian Court signed a consultation on the nullity of the sentence and the acts of the Council of Embrun. Indeed, in our age of the century, a great blindness has befallen an innumerable multitude of Christians, who, alas, are found to be more beastly than the beasts. Yet I do not wish this to be understood of everyone. For the beasts themselves provide for the future, anticipating harm and pursuing benefits. This is evident in ants, in cranes, and in wild geese, which, as the harshness of winter approaches, either flee to warmer places or collect food for themselves in caves and hollows. This happens by an instinct of nature. Rational men, not ignoring the future punishments of winter, whether eternal or most bitter temporary ones, with open eyes desire to foresee nothing to avert them, thinking that for them the name of faith alone suffices for salvation. Of whom Paul says: "They profess that they know God, but in their works they deny him." We read of Saint Jerome, on his own testimony, that when he was intent upon secular letters and was carried away in an ecstasy, he was asked who he was. He replied: "I am a Christian." And he heard: "You lie. You are a Ciceronian, not a Christian." And having been gravely whipped, he swore that he would not wish to read such books thereafter. O, would that the inquiry might now reach many Christians, so that the answer could be: "You are not a Christian, but a pagan." For many are found whose conduct differs little from the loves of the pagans, who worship idols made by hand. I wrote to <term>Tyro</term> <gloss>a proper name</gloss> with as many words as I could, and I also instructed him that he should not think the matter was to be held with him alone as much as with me, for I had been the author and guarantor of all things that had been arranged between us. I also urged him with many reasons to delay the entire matter until my arrival, and to yield to that friendship which, as it was first with his master, so afterwards was it with me. I warned him with many words that my reasons and the respect for our ancient friendship should have more weight with him than the seditions and hatreds of <term>Saturnius</term> <gloss>a proper name</gloss>. I promised that if he were persuaded by me, he would receive great gratitude from me. But if truly the evil counsels of seditious men had overcome my hope, I reminded him that I would omit nothing that would pertain to your defense and my own extraction. I think he will credit me more than Saturnius, and if my counsel should deceive me in this matter, I will see to it that he repents his action. I await his letters daily. If anything is done by him in the meantime which falls uncomfortably for you, you should make me aware. Farewell.

It is no small matter, nor an unusual one, about which I had long ago decided to write to you. Everyone is complaining, to state the matter in one word, that you have made wolves the guardians of the sheep. <note>A red decorative initial 'A' marks the beginning of the text.</note>Although these things about which I write to you are not so new or unusual that something of this kind has never happened to men before, they have nevertheless aroused no small admiration due to the opinion that people will hold. Vecturius, a man (as you know) once considered to be among the most wealthy of our citizens, had badly mismanaged his own affairs and contracted a large amount of debt. And yet, he had kept this so hidden that neither his close associates nor those who loved the man were aware of it. What he did afterward was suitable; since his fortune could no longer support him, the matter would perhaps have been settled in some year. Having collected his goods from all sides as secretly as he could, he pretended to go abroad and promised he would return in time for the first day of August, the very calends he had sworn by. He urged all of us who cared for him to provide surety on his behalf, in case anyone should happen to summon him to court. We believed that he was bound by no debt, or only by a very small one. And even if he were bound by a large one, we thought he was capable of paying it. What more is there to say? I gave bail for him. Then he departed. But when the day of the trial arrived, and this man did not appear (as in good faith he ought to have), we were soon after held to answer for the debt by the creditors. When we inquired about him and begged the judges to grant us an extension of time, and I learned that our plea was going to be granted, it became necessary for me to pay on his behalf. The sum of money which he owed to his creditors was paid out. Even if this matter had been quite inconvenient for others, it was so grave for me that I never hope to be able to pay off the debt which I incurred for his sake. I would never have thought it possible that such a man could have fallen into such destitution, that he would attack his own people with such machinations and deceits. Thus the matter stands, that trust is given to those who possess no shame or modesty. Others are very

From this you can understand, that never were the foundations of our republic laid under better auspices than on this present day. For when formerly our <term>senatus</term> <gloss>senate</gloss> used to gather to consult about matters of the highest importance, everyone served the time. If anyone wished to divide opinions, there was no one who dared to contribute freely what he felt. Now, however, we are led with such great zeal toward a liberty that is not feigned or shadowy (as it once was), but we have received from our ancestors such that we should never live unless at this time in which we now exist. For, with the few who were oppressing public liberty removed from the city, all use equal law. It is permitted for everyone to speak about our republic and what he feels, and to feel freely what he says. The pursuits that were applied to private matters have all been turned toward the distinction of the republic. And they are especially intent on this one thing: which of them might best benefit the city. If, therefore, you desire to be considered great among your own, come to this republic of ours, which we hold to be most excellent and beautiful. <note>A red decorative initial 'O' at the beginning of the text.</note>Leaving aside all other things, I have completed with great zeal all matters that I understood pertained to you, and I am writing to you now to describe the order in which I have conducted these affairs. As soon as I arrived in the province, I immediately made inquiries of the local people as to whether the route for merchants was still open. Having been sufficiently informed by them on this matter, I took myself to Alexandria. After your first goods were dispatched and I had taken care of everything regarding my own affairs that I knew pertained to yours, I ensured that the time, which was very short for your other business, was not spent in idleness. I gathered cargo from all sides, and I brought those items that were most suitable for shipping into the harbor. On the second of March, when everything had already been stowed on the ship, the sailors set out from the port. Since the winds were favorable, almost all of them raised their sails at the same time. What followed from that was reported to me not long after; at most, only two or three ships reached the shore, if any of those belonged to you. The others, as it was said, suffered shipwreck. It is understood that they have not yet departed from that port for fear of the storm, and they will make the journey to us as soon as that storm subsides. May our messages result in good fortune. I wished for these things to be known to you primarily through our triremes, so that you might be better informed about all your affairs and might set aside all anxiety, if perhaps you have conceived any from this shipwreck. Since you are a prudent man in all other matters, there is nothing for which I need to admonish you. For you can judge for yourself that the goods are worth much more, even had there been no shipwreck. I will expedite the rest when the time comes. If you wish for me to do anything else regarding your affairs, please signify it to me by your letters. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the second paragraph.</note>Nothing could be added to this anxiety of yours. You have acted so that even if all things had gone to ruin, I would still have been grateful to you, since your business could not have been conducted with greater zeal than that with which you have conducted my affairs at this time.

Now, however, I do not merely desire them; for I already strive so to apply myself to them that there can be nothing in life that is strong enough to distract me from them. I desire, therefore, to be joined to you as a companion and student. Formerly, there was a different reason and institution of life, while my wife, children, and parents were alive. And my mind was never set toward these things; nor, had it been, would it have been permitted with piety intact. Now, however, since I have been deprived by death of almost all those necessary to me, and I have lost those who helped me bear all troubles, even if I should be saddened by them, I hope to be with you shortly. Meanwhile, I will settle my affairs, as they say, and since I am more free and ready for that kind of life which I embrace with the greatest heart, I will extract myself from these impediments that have held me captive until now, so that there will be no greater care for me than to care for nothing except divine things. Now, however, it would be most shameful to neglect this <note>that is, the practice of friendship</note> through a lack of either virtue or learnedness, which I have often preferred above many and very great things. I will state the reason that has impelled me to this. For I have persuaded myself either that there is no good in life, or that it is something conjoined with friendship. And if this were to occur through our own zeal alone, I would not admire this good so much. But when I see that all people are led by nature itself and driven by a certain impulse to live together and to love one another, there is no one who does not judge this thing to be divine. For not everyone arrives at friendship equally; rather, each person accommodates himself more rightly and better to them according to how much he excels in virtue and talent. For we see the varying pursuits of men; some hope for utility in friends, others for honors. Some are moved to these things so that they may have those with whom they may amuse themselves. The wise man, however, places all the fruit of friendship in honesty. And I, when I had decided to love, not through good men, took care not to follow any others than those I understood to be pleasing for their own sake. I was afterward so attentive in that matter that I took care of one thing: that I should not be surpassed in duty by any of my own. I will tell you what is true: I love men so that they may be pleased. I never love more than when good things happen to my friends. <note>A red decorative initial N begins the paragraph.</note>I have never considered any danger or labor so great that I should think it ought to be avoided for the benefit of friends. Nor do I judge any other thing so great (virtue excepted) as friendship, which I hold must be preferred. I think you also know this. For by guessing from my own fate, you know we had the same teacher. Even after we departed from school, our friendship grew with the years. For whether we were in public affairs or private matters, whether in the city or in the country, we always maintained a great partnership between us, just as a king does with his advisors. Yet there has never been a time in which, by the mutual exchange of our feelings, you could find your duty toward me lacking. I hope that your fortune may remain and that you suffer no unworthy insult. But if anything should happen to your affairs, you would understand what kind of heart I have for you. I ask and even beseech you, with greater insistence, that since I love you so much, you do not allow the envy of men to tear our friendship asunder. May the memory of our friendship, which began in our boyhood, prevail more with you than the voices of those who, at this time, strive as much as they can to diminish our friendship. For I desire that we not only remain in friendship, but also that we be judged as men who are surpassed by no other in love and benevolence. Farewell.

But concerning the modesty and humanity that you write to me about that I should have toward my equals, I will endeavor with such zeal that I may seem to depart in no new way of life from them. And I hope for good things in the future. For the more ambitious I am in my studies, the more grace and benevolence I will obtain among all. There is nothing else that I should write to you, except that you remind me with your letters. For as often as I read them, I see myself being and talking with you. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial letter 'O'</note>Everyone expects your presence and your service. From this you can understand that even your enemies desire greatly to return into your favor. If you neglect this, you will neither consult your own reputation, nor will you fail the expectation of all your fellow citizens. For the matter stands in such a way that, even if you did not have the means, you could nevertheless persuade no one to the contrary. Therefore, it must be worked upon, and with your whole heart you must focus on satisfying the will of your fellow citizens. Nothing can adhere better to your nature, nor be more worthy of praise by industry, than that you should present yourself to men, and desire those things which you understand are desired by men. For it is clearly said by the <term>Stoics</term> <gloss>a school of Hellenistic philosophy</gloss> that all things on earth were created for the sake of humans, but humans for the sake of humans.

And let neither labor nor danger deter us from that thing. For either there is no other way to immortality, or it is located primarily in this place, so that for the sake of the welfare of good men, for the cause of friends, we may not be broken by any hardships, and let us offer ourselves not only to those whom we ought to love and protect, but also be conciliatory to them, and excusable to enemies. If you remember how much each of us ought to suffer, I will rejoice for you, and I will rejoice greatly for you if I understand that my letters have added something to your talent and virtue, that you may achieve more maturely all those things which you see being sought by you with great zeal. <note>A red decorative initial letter N</note>I would have thought that I had done enough for the public interest and my friends, had I not expected that you would admonish me in that matter, which, since it is honorable among others, would also be necessary for me. But since I have already advanced in my age in public matters, and have never fled from any labors or dangers for its sake, I seemed to myself, without injury to my country, to have betaken myself to leisure as if to a certain port of our life. And this was to be conceded by all citizens and my intimates, so that I, who for a long time sailed on the sea, might finally place myself in the port. But it is such that, as in other things, so in friendship and the love of one's country, there is a certain excessive greed and desire of men, which can never be satisfied. I do not know what more either my country or my friends wish for themselves, than that I should again repeat the troubles of my old age, and since I am still able to live for myself for some time, I should seem to have plunged my hands into them. Do not (if you love me) exhort me to that matter which is fitting neither for this age nor for these studies of mine. For our republic has enough of protection if it uses the counsels of those citizens for whom it is useful. For me, however, quiet should be obtained, deserved by my past merits in the republic. You, however, if you defend the cause of friends among the citizens, I hold greater thanks to you than if you had interrupted my leisure. Farewell.

For such discomforts surround me that I see no exit, except that which delay might bring me. I am now so miserable that Fortune has complete power, wherever it might strike me. I have lost my homeland, in which I long flourished with honor and dignity. My paternal property has been taken from me. The companions I had in the republic have been carried off by the force of civil wars. All who were my friends have either perished or are in the same calamity as I. What more remains for me, a miserable man, than to put an end to so many evils through death? Believe me, I am not only lacking counsel, but I seem to myself to have become foolish. I used to relieve my mental sickness by reading or writing; now, however, there are no arts that bring me any delight. I desire your presence most of all. I hope that either by grieving with me or by consoling me, you will bring me some relief in such great sorrow. It could not be (given the prudence and wisdom you have always possessed) that there would be no counsel from you as to how I might endure all things less bitterly. Since you are able to do so, strive to come here; if tasks detain you, write something...

<note>A red decorative initial Q is illuminated.</note> How much your letter has afflicted me with sorrow, to the point that I myself am in great need of consolation! Just as our feelings were wont to be uplifted in times of ease, so afterwards, when things were disturbed and cast down—the things in which you had long flourished among your fellow citizens—I feel no less turmoil in my own spirit, as if everything that happened to your affairs had happened to my own; and what is more, what is mine is yours. You have in me a companion and participant in your hardships more than a consoler. But where there is such strength and magnitude of intellect, as yours is, that you are able to console yourself from your own letters and from my comfort, you have certainly brought some aid to both of us at the same time. But I am not sufficient for this task, nor was I ever a suitable teacher for such a matter. What I can easily do, I shall achieve. In the first few days I will come to you, and if grief relieves sorrow (which kind of consolation would be foreign), I will not omit anything in diminishing your grief. Meanwhile, however, you will borrow some counsel from letters and philosophy, and you will remember that you are a man. For since you are considered the wisest among almost all men living in this age of ours, consider how it conforms to the expectation of those who know you, that you are being overcome by grief, you who have always borne prosperous Fortune with modesty. I do not write this from myself. But since the eyes of many are cast upon you, I often hear the conversations of men being held about you. I, however, reply to that, that it is impossible for you not to feel such a calamity and loss of things. But still, for the sake of your wisdom, you bear all things with a calm mind. Nor do I think that counsel is lacking to you, nor a remedy, to heal this sickness. You will therefore do what I desire most in this sorrow of yours. You will stand with an upright spirit, and by enduring, you will conquer Fortune which previously conquered you. If you have done this, you will certainly derive greater glory from your victory than from all

<note>A decorative red initial 'L' marks the beginning of the text.</note> I recently read the letters you sent to me, from which I received great distress of mind. But I am angry with you because you wrote so late to me about your extreme poverty. For I judge that if this had been written to me in time, I could have devoted effort to our friends so that your poverty would not have been so long and burdensome to you. As I see and as you write to me, shame was an impediment to you, and that is a vice of all nobility, which considers it no less shameful to beg for assistance from another in times of need than to be in want. You will blame yourself if, while friends were unaware, you suffered longer than you should have from this trouble. What is pressing, I will take care of, so that in the future you will not be in such discomfort as you have been up to now, and so that you might proceed with such modesty that neither excessive shame will harm you, nor negligence on the part of your friends. I am sending you a small amount of money, until better provision can be made by me and our friends. Do not, I beg you, despair of your friends. I, as I say regarding myself, will see to it that in no way, while I have abundance, will I allow you to suffer from any lack of life's necessities. I judge that all who loved you for your own sake know this. Farewell.

<note>A decorative red initial 'A' marks the beginning of the text.</note> That I have been reduced to poverty, which I see happens to many, I bear with a mind somewhat more elevated than my fortune. But since all my studies, by doing well for many, have fallen into ruin, I cannot be sufficiently satisfied. How could I have been led to the point where I would be treated poorly by those for whom I have been thrifty and liberal? You know well enough what benefits and services our fellow citizens have received from me. How ungrateful they have been toward me, time itself has taught. For when those men whom I had made my friends for the sake of our common salvation had turned against me, and had instigated judges and prepared false witnesses against me, who was there to defend my rights? Or who was willing to protect my dignity? But I feel that it happens with good reason that I experience them as ungrateful, in whose love for me there was no rationale. For I know and understand that what is in the old proverb is true.

<summary>In the first letter, the author reprimands a friend for delaying news of their poverty due to misplaced shame, promising immediate financial support and assistance. The second letter laments the author's personal ruin and the ingratitude of those he formerly supported, reflecting on the cruelty of fortune and the betrayal of false friends.</summary>
<keywords>Gasparino, poverty, friendship, ingratitude, humanism, moral philosophy, fortune</keywords>

And if the matter could return to its previous state, I would certainly regret this turn of events. Meanwhile, I am burdened by anxiety. But this is nothing compared to them. I have written to you, not so that you might expect my counsel and aid in a desperate situation, but because I feel my pain is lightened when I speak with you about my troubles. Farewell.</meta>

<note>A large red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the letter.</note> It is no new thing you write to me, nor is it unknown to me. For how often have you believed that I, by the indignity of such fortune, have frequently seen myself and other citizens, both honest and distinguished, endure things beyond what is good and fair? Although this calamity of ours is nothing compared to yours, it happens nevertheless (I know not how) that we feel less burdened by the troubles that are common in the city. I would prefer, however, that you seek aid for this distress from your own wisdom rather than from common habit. For I know this will be the result: that nothing will more alleviate your grief than the realization that none of these things happened to you because of your own merit. And your opinion, as it is now, will change greatly if you take more account of your own virtues than of the distress that is still fresh. You write to me, not for the sake of aid or counsel in a desperate matter, but because it helps you to speak with me about your troubles. You do what is customary among friends. I am accustomed to doing the same. I know that I am unburdened in spirit when I have revealed my every distress to my friends. For this, I am most grateful, and I thank you that you have chosen me from among many to whom you might entrust your cares. By these and other signs, I judge that I am greatly loved by you. As for the rest that pertains to your consolation, you yourself will see to it better (as I hope) through your own virtue than through my letters. Farewell.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>Additionally, following the general council of <term>Innocentius</term> <gloss>Pope Innocent IV</gloss>, religious orders also were confirmed by the Apostolic See. Those who, through the Council of Lyon under Pope <term>Gregorius X</term>, admitted some to their profession, or newly assumed a house or some place, or alienated houses or places which they hold without special license of the Apostolic See, are excommunicated <note>citing the Sext Decretals, Book 3, Title 24, Chapter 1</note>.

¶ The second principal has two orders outside the clergy, as in the book <term>De Periculosis</term> <gloss>On Dangerous Things</gloss>, in the Sext.

¶ First: a religious who rashly lays aside the habit of his religion in schools or elsewhere is excommunicated as an apostate from his religion, as noted in the Decretals. Indeed, it is said in the <term>Panormitanus</term> <gloss>Niccolò de' Tedeschi, a prominent canon lawyer</gloss>: if a religious lays aside the habit for a base reason, such as to go to a brothel at night, he incurs this; but otherwise if he does not lay aside the habit but hides it underneath or covers it with something else so he is not recognized, especially if he does it for a good reason—for instance, because it is hot and he does not wish to be recognized as belonging to his religion, provided he still wears the religious habit underneath. Whoever lays it aside out of fear of robbers does not lay it aside rashly. Nor are those excused who change their habit in schools so they do not appear as religious. Whoever lays it aside out of playful levity for a moment, to run or throw a stone, does not incur it, because it is probable that he did not intend to violate the canons in those minor matters, so as to fall into such snares.

¶ The second is against religious who attend the studies of the friars without the counsel of their superior and the agreement of their convent, or unless permission for such study has been granted by a majority of the convent. This is to be understood when one goes to schools outside the city; however, it is not necessary for a meeting to be called regarding schools of the same city, and the license of the abbot suffices.

¶ Also, this is understood of those who actually reside in the convent, for those who are outside with the sole license of the abbot may go to schools.

¶ The third principal contains those cases and incidents of religious who defraud or evade the tithes owed to churches, and if they do not desist within a month after being requested by those to whom it pertains, or if they do not make restitution of those usurped or retained within two months, they are suspended from their offices, administrations, and benefices; those not holding such are excommunicated.

¶ Therefore, the first case is that religious who presume to appropriate to themselves novales <note>land recently brought into cultivation</note> or other tithes owed to churches, which for any legitimate reason do not belong to them, or who usurp them by contrived frauds or guises.

The third, those who buy animals in many places for the purpose of defrauding churches, and then deliver them to sellers or others to be held by them. The fourth, those who, regarding tithes of land which they deliver to others to be cultivated, do not allow the tithes to be paid to the churches, or forbid it, unless requested as discussed above in <term>De decimis</term> <gloss>On Tithes</gloss>, chapter 1, <term>m. cle.</term> <gloss>a reference to a Clementine canon</gloss>.

The fourth principal concerning the state of the clergy, chapter 1, § <term>Quia vero</term> <gloss>Because, indeed</gloss>, sets forth two points: that monks or regular canons <note>members of religious orders bound by vows</note> not having administration of others' affairs should not presume to offer themselves to the courts of princes without the special license of their superiors. If, however, they presume to offer themselves to said courts so that they inflict any damage upon these prelates and monasteries, we will that they incur a sentence of excommunication <term>ipso facto</term> <gloss>by the very fact itself</gloss>, says the text. Two things are therefore necessary to incur this excommunication: that the court has been entered, and that there is a cause for damaging the monastery or prelate. From the mere act of leaving the cloister for this reason, one is not bound. 

The second case concerns monks who, within the enclosure of the monastery, hold arms without the license of their abbots, says the text. For <term>Johannes Andreae</term> <gloss>a prominent 14th-century canonist</gloss>, on the word "holding," says that one coming from outside to the cloister with arms, with no intention of holding them, or who does not hold them by deliberate act, does not seem to be bound; the word implies acting with effect. 

The fifth principal concerns those hindering the visitors of nuns in their visitations through forbidden methods, in <term>Clementinae</term>, <term>De statu clericorum</term> <gloss>On the state of the clergy</gloss>, chapter 2, at the end; unless the guilty party repents. The gloss of <term>Johannes Andreae</term> suggests that it is necessary for the impediment to proceed and for a warning to follow. 

The sixth principal, in <term>De religiosis domibus</term> <gloss>On religious houses</gloss>, chapter 1, in the <term>Clementinae</term>, contains two cases. The first condemns the state of the <term>Beguines</term> <gloss>lay religious women living in semi-monastic communities</gloss> and excommunicates those following it or newly assuming it. The second excommunicates religious who provide counsel, help, or favor regarding them. general, Book 6. ¶ The ninth principal is against those who presume to despoil clerics or any other ecclesiastical persons, to whom pertains the election in any churches, monasteries, or other pious places, or the blood relatives of the same, or their churches, monasteries, or places, by taking their goods for themselves or through others, or otherwise unjustly persecuting them, for the reason that those, when asked or otherwise induced, refused to elect the person for whom they were asked or induced to elect. <term>Extra de electione</term> <gloss>Decretals on election</gloss>, <term>Sciant cuncti</term> <gloss>Let all know</gloss>, Book 6. ¶ The tenth principal contains three cases. The first is against those who have caused any Christians to be killed by others. The second is against those who have ordered this to be done, even if death does not follow from it. The third is against those who receive, defend, or hide others. <term>Extra de homicidio</term> <gloss>Decretals on homicide</gloss>, <term>c. per humani</term> <gloss>chapter "by human"</gloss>, Book 6. ¶ The eleventh principal has two cases. The first is against those who have granted reprisals or seizures <note>actions to seize property as compensation</note> where one is burdened for another against ecclesiastical persons or their goods. The second is against those who have procured reprisals for such people, that is, ecclesiastical persons, which are not granted by custom or use, unless they have revoked such a presumption within a month, to be calculated from the time of the grant or extortion. <term>Extra de iniuriis</term> <gloss>Decretals on injuries</gloss>, <term>c. de pignorationibus</term> <gloss>chapter on seizures</gloss>, Book 6. ¶ The twelfth principal contains two. The first is against those who, because of excommunication, suspension, or interdict sentences promulgated against kings, princes, barons, nobles, bailiffs, or ministers of any kind, or against any others, have given license to others to kill them, to capture them, or otherwise to act against their persons or their goods, or who protected those who delivered such sentences, or those who were the occasion of them, or those who observed such sentences, or those wishing to excommunicate such excommunicated persons, unless they have revoked the license while the matter is still intact, or if the process of capturing goods occurred on the occasion of such a license, unless they have restored the goods or provided satisfaction for them within eight days. The thirteenth principal contains two, and both are reserved to the Pope. The first is regarding the penalty <note>original: "de pe."</note> in the Clementines, chapter: if anyone <note>original: "si qs."</note>, as to whether someone has injuriously or rashly struck a pontiff, or seized, or banished him, or ordered this to be done, or approved that it was done by others, or was an associate of the perpetrator in these acts, or provided counsel or favor in these things, or knowingly defended the same person. In those cases of the aforesaid, in which they would not otherwise incur the canons published regarding the penalty. The Gloss on the word "of the aforesaid" <note>original: "de predictis"</note> as in the one banishing, or ordering it, or an associate having ratified it, etc., as follows. The second principal <note>original: "ptas" (potestas)</note> is regarding the councilors, aldermen, advocates, rectors, consuls, and officials of the same person, by whatever name they may be known, being guilty in the aforementioned matters; they incur excommunication reserved to the Popes, except in the article of death, in the Clementines, concerning the penalty, chapter one. 

The fourteenth principal is also reserved to the Pope: those temporal lords who compel others to celebrate divine services in an interdicted place, or who, through heralds, cause the people to be evacuated to hear those services, or forbid that publicly excommunicated or interdicted persons, upon being warned that they should depart from the churches where masses are celebrated, leave, or if they themselves, having been notified and warned, do not depart, they are excommunicated in the Clementines, concerning the sentence of excommunication, chapter: whoever <note>original: "quis."</note>. 

The fifteenth principal is in the Clementines, concerning usury, chapter: he who <note>original: "ex. gui"</note>. It contains six cases: namely, cities and officials doing so; behold the first. Dictating; behold the second. Or writing statutes regarding usury to be paid, not to be reclaimed, or not restored; behold the third. Or judging according to those; behold the fourth. Or not deleting them from the books of the city if they could within three months; behold the fifth. Or aiding in them; behold the sixth. They are excommunicated. Likewise, the same sentences are incurred by any powers of those cities, captains, rectors, consuls, judges, councilors, or other officials attempting the aforesaid. 

The sixteenth principal contains six in the Clementines, concerning consanguinity and affinity, chapter: unique. Namely, contracting marriage in a degree of consanguinity; behold the first. And of prohibited affinity; behold the second. Or with a nun; behold the third. He is excommunicated. The same is the case regarding religious persons doing so, and nuns, and also clerics placed in sacred orders; behold again the other three cases. And the gloss says that this is constituted only in the aforementioned cases.

<note>A red paragraph mark (pilcrow) indicates the beginning of the sixth and seventh rules.</note>

The sixth rule: when about to hear women, the confessor should take care that while he purifies their souls from vices, he himself does not become defiled by voluntary pleasures. He should not be like a towel that becomes dirty while washing others; rather, he should be like soap, which becomes clean by cleansing others. Therefore, he should not consider himself a respecter of persons, believing that he listens more freely and easily to beautiful or young women than to old women in confession. Instead, he should fortify himself with good and holy imaginations. First, by considering that he ought to be an angel of God and a vicar of the trembling God in judgment. Then, turning the eyes of his body and the lights of his soul away from the women, he should see their souls, as if they were lepers or wounded by the dire demons of mortal sins, or at least wrinkled or scabrous from venial offenses, which must be healed by the blood of Christ and the sacrament of penance. The confessor should secretly make the sign of the cross with his thumb upon his own person, for the sake of preserving purity. He should invoke God with at least a brief prayer or short petition. He should avoid, without necessity, sweet words and any useless, idle chatter. Thus, he should apply himself solely to the honor of God and the salvation of the soul of the other, firmly and appropriately. Nor should he despair if he is tempted while resisting the pleasure of the flesh, mindful of what Christ said to the disciples: "If they drink any deadly thing, it will not hurt them." <note>Mark 16:18</note> He removes the appearance of evil, etc. Regarding which, the blessed Gregory <note>Pope Gregory I</note> says: "Priests, by their good exhortations, take malice away from the hearts of others; they remove the appearance of evil, and while they hear poisonous conversations and do not deviate toward perverse prayers, it is a deadly thing they drink, and it will not hurt them." The same is advised in his *Pastoral Care*, where he says: "It happens frequently that while a rector's soul recognizes the temptations of another, through hearing those temptations, he himself is struck by them; but these things are not to be feared by the pastor, who so easily snatches his own away and who, out of mercy, is fatigued by the temptation of another." Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> also makes this clear in the *Summa*, Part 4, saying that the prayer he gives in the sacrament of penance restores him, if any inclination to sin should come from the circumstance of the conversation, that is, from necessary carnal speech, either in the one confessing or in the confessor. 

The seventh rule: the confessor should not look at the face of the one confessing, especially if it is a woman, so that the penitent does not blush and so that the confessor is not wounded in his soul by the feminine gaze. <note>The text ends with a truncated Latin phrase suggesting "spiritual surgeon/physician" but the manuscript is cut off at *cyrologi*.</note>

<summary>The text details guidelines for confessors hearing the confessions of women, emphasizing the avoidance of temptation, the maintenance of professional detachment, and the necessity of focusing on the spiritual healing of the penitent.</summary>
<keywords>Confession, Penance, Confessor, Temptation, Purity, Pastoral Care, Johannes Nider</keywords>

X.text:
<meta>continues from previous page: ...as according to that saying of Habakkuk: "A burning wind shall face him." <note>Habakkuk 1:9</note> Hence the gloss upon that passage in Genesis: "She saw that the tree was delightful to the eyes," <note>Genesis 3:6</note> says: "Lest we be slippery in thought, we must not gaze upon what it is not lawful to covet; for just as a pure mind is accustomed to be in the thought of its own lascivious pleasure, so the eyes must be filled as though they were certain spoilers of guilt." For Eve would not have touched the tree if she had not first looked at it incautiously. It must be considered how much we ought to restrain ourselves from illicit things, since we live in such a mortal way that if we live by the eyes of the living, we come to death.</meta>

A stable rule: the confessor must take the greatest care that at the beginning of the confession, and especially during its progress, he is not sad, austere, or rigid, <note>harsh or unyielding</note> for this is very rare with penitents, whether they are timid or simple. For soon it will close the mouth of the sinner, but he should be kind and mild in the manner of a prudent physician, and affable. Therefore, before anyone begins to confess who is not accustomed to confessing—as is true of many among the bashful and the young—he may say things to open the confession, and if the matter so requires, he should ask about their homeland or children, so that whoever wishes to confess may take the courage to speak. For some people, out of bashfulness, at the beginning lose all memory of what is to be confessed, especially the young and women who rarely confess. Then he should proceed to other instructions that follow.

This is shown by the one whose place the confessor holds, Christ, when he says: "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick." <note>Matthew 9:12</note> Thus he himself acted, who did not abhor sinners and publicans in the city, but called them to penance; for the Son of Man came not to call the just, but sinners. <note>Matthew 9:13</note>

Concerning women, he should have this habit: he should not dwell long, unless the necessity of the confession requires it. Those who call out frequently, and those who want to confess often, should be kept away from such excessive and useless frequency, and a fixed time should be assigned to them for confessing, so that at other times he does not hear them, nor should he ever expose himself to other frequent conversations. And he should use harsh and rigid words toward them rather than soft ones. For as the venerable Bonaventure says, such women, and those like them, not knowing themselves or the priests, infect them incredibly; without the loss of time, they fall, and with the *preciosa* <gloss>precious</gloss> time, they waste too much. Concerning the aforementioned rigor of words, Christ taught when he said to his most holy mother: "What is it to me and to thee? My hour has not yet come." <note>John 2:4</note> Nevertheless, he showed kindness toward sinners.

<summary>This page outlines the behavioral standards for a confessor, stressing the need for a kind and approachable demeanor to put penitents at ease while warning against excessive or unnecessary conversations with women.</summary>

Regarding such persons, however, those who had accepted something as a gift and had consumed it before they understood the truth of the matter are not held to restore it. 

Similarly, an exception is made when someone handles the case of those who have been despoiled <note>the original Latin term is <term>spoliatorum</term>, referring to those who have been stripped of their goods</note> by warning and inducing, as much as they are able, the <term>raptor</term> <gloss>robber/plunderer</gloss> to make restitution, especially if there is a probable hope of the correction of the plunderers, and when the plunderer is rendered unable to make restitution in whole or in large part by such corruption. Those who therefore insist at opportune hours so that the plunderer may restore the stolen goods are not held to restore them. 

Under the second case also: those who know or probably believe that, because of their company or association with the robbers or the bringing or carrying away of others, the robbers themselves did not do more than they otherwise would have done, and yet they had and spent something of the stolen goods, such persons are held to restore what they had or spent, and also for all the <term>dampnum</term> <gloss>damage/harm</gloss> which they or anyone of their family caused directly or occasionally. 

The third: when several do damage together, and even if one without the other, or several without this one, would have done it, such a person is held to pay pro rata, that is, for his own portion. This is how much he contributed to the total damage if the damage that he himself caused cannot be distinguished from that which others caused. In this estimation, however, the judgment must be held that whoever is more strenuous and whoever struck more fear and terror into the enemies should also be held more. 

Likewise also in the case when some associate with robbers and believe that the robbers would have done the damage even without their help or instigation, but they are held at least to that which they probably believe they did because of their instigation or help. 

The fourth: if any associate with the robbers and do not cooperate with them in doing any damage, yet they are in mind prepared to defend [the robbers] if by chance those being despoiled had wished to defend their property from the plunderers, and because of their presence and that of their associates, [the victims] did not dare to resist those despoiling, or setting fire to their houses, and if anyone has associated [with the robbers], he cannot be free from restitution. Indeed, if some go with the robbers with the intention of pacifying, they are not excused unless they signify this to the adversaries, because otherwise the adversaries, out of fear of them, would not dare to defend their own property. Hence it is the same as if they helped them. Second, if they incited the adversaries, which then seems to be in the first case. Whoever was the cause of the entire damage is held <term>in solidum</term> <gloss>for the whole amount</gloss>, that is, for the entire damage. This is the case where there were several robbers, of whom no one induced another to join, nor did any lord <note>referring to a feudal superior or leader</note> order it, but each says he acts for himself; if they go as if they were one army, each is held <term>in solidum</term> <gloss>for the whole amount</gloss>, because in such a case each helped the others and made them stronger, and all are co-perpetrators. Otherwise, if they did not go together but each was separately doing damage, each is held for what he did, understanding beyond what has already been said that one would not dare or be able to do the damage without the other; otherwise, each is held even for the part of the damage that he willed. 

Note also that stolen or plundered property must be restored with all the fruits and profits that it yielded, or which could have been yielded, because they are held to <term>interesse</term> <gloss>compensation for damages/interest</gloss> and for all damages. Nor is one excused if the item perished while in his possession, because he was in default of restoration; if, however, he wished to return it to the owner and the owner refused to accept it, he is excused. Furthermore, regarding any damage where restitution is to be made, since the one causing damage unjustly is held to restore the item, he is also held for <term>interesse</term> <gloss>compensation for damages/interest</gloss>, that is, for the valuation of the damage, and for the fruits perceived from the item if the item was fruit-bearing, though not for the fruit that came from the industry of the one who is using that item. Where a <term>vsurarius</term> <gloss>usurer</gloss> or another person causing damage to another by imposing usury, and a poor man is forced to sell his grain for less, or someone has lost a profit or trade profit from which he lived while he was a laborer, he is held for the expenses of doctors, damages, labor, and his dependents <note>literally: daughter(s), but often used in legal contexts for family members/dependents</note> to the <term>interesse</term> <gloss>compensation for damages/interest</gloss>, unless the one suffering the damage, being asked, voluntarily remits it. However, a usurer is not held to restore money or [profits] acquired through usurious money, that is, the usury or the money which he had through that usury. Hope of the Lord of majesty. Venerable and tender mother of the heavenly King. Holy and sweet, kind Lady of the angels, you are the gate of paradise. You are the ladder of the heavenly kingdom and of glory, you are the bridal chamber, you are the ark of piety and grace. You are the fountain of mercy, you are the spouse and mother of the eternal King. You are the temple and sanctuary of the Holy Spirit: the noble dining room of the entire most blessed Trinity. You are the mediatrix of God and men, lover of mortals, illuminator of the heavenly ones. You are the <note>original: "agamissatrix" likely a corruption or variant for "agonizantium" (those in struggle/agony)</note> advocate for those in struggle: the merciful one for the poor: and the refuge of sinners. Tenth, I have sinned because I did not care for the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. In me there is no wisdom <note>original: "sapiā"</note> to contemplate divine things. In me there is no fortitude to resist temptations, tribulations, and evil thoughts. In me there is no piety to sympathize with the poor and the afflicted in heart and work. By that terror which, hanging on the cross, You made formidable to the serpent, the devil, and acceptable to friends and placating to enemies, grant that I may rejoice in Your peace and in the present and future prosperity of the entire Church.

<note>A red decorative initial 'G'.</note>I give thanks to your immense majesty and eternal piety, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who has deigned to satisfy me, your unworthy servant and miserable sinner, not because my merits demand it, but by your many and great mercies, with the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. X.text:
<note>A red paragraph mark (pilcrow) precedes the text.</note>May this most holy sacrament of the body and blood of your beloved son, our Lord Jesus Christ, be, I ask, holy Father, the sweetness and delight of my soul, my salvation and holiness in every temptation, my peace and joy in every tribulation, my light and strength in every word and deed, and my solace and final protection in death. And I pray that through this I may deserve to be filled with your holy spirit, directed along the way of your commandments, and that I may be refreshed by this same viaticum <note>original: "viatico", the Eucharist given to the dying</note> at the final moment of my life, and that being refreshed now, I may be preserved until then without interruption, and led by your holy angels to that place where you yourself are the true light for your saints, full contentment, complete joy, and perfect, everlasting happiness. Through the same Christ our Lord. Amen. <note>A red paragraph mark (pilcrow) precedes "Agimus".</note>We give you thanks for all those who have been beatified, asking to be aided by their intercession. <note>A red paragraph mark (pilcrow) precedes "Pro".</note>Moreover, for those who are in the places of purgatory <note>original: "purgatorijs locis"</note>, the Son offers himself to you, Father, supplicating that through this most holy host their punishment may be lighter and shorter. <note>A red paragraph mark (pilcrow) precedes "Pro".</note>For us, however, whom the sins of flesh and blood still weigh down, the Son offers himself to you, supplicating that the blood of your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, may wash away, and his flesh may cleanse, the sins that we have contracted from flesh and blood. Amen. <note>A large red decorative initial "A" appears at the bottom.</note>Hail, most holy flesh, highest sweetness of life.

Now what I have sought, I see; what I have desired, I hold; I languish with the love of Jesus and burn entirely in my heart.
Say, love burns continuously, sweetens wonderfully, itself purely and delightfully delights and makes happy.
Say, love sent from heaven clings to me in my marrow; it kindles the mind deeply; here the spirit is delighted.
O blessed conflagration, O burning desire, O sweet refreshment: to love the Son of God.
When Jesus is thus loved, this love is not extinguished, nor does it grow tepid, nor does it die, but it grows when it arrives.
Jesus, flower of the Mother Virgin, love of our sweetness, to You be praise, honor of divinity, kingdom of beatitude.
Come, come, most excellent King, Father of immense glory, and shine clearly more joyfully, now expected more often.
Jesus, more serene than the sun and sweeter than balsam, sweeter than all sweetness, more lovable than all things.
By whom love so affects me, and whose fragrance so refreshes me, in whom my mind faints; He alone suffices for the lover.
You are the delight of the mind, the plumage of love, You are my glory, Jesus, salvation of the world.
My beloved, return, consort of the Father’s right hand; You have quickly conquered the enemy, now enjoy the kingdom of heaven.
I will follow wherever You go, nor can I be taken away when You have stolen my heart; Jesus, praise of our race.
Citizens of heaven, meet Him, lift up your gates.

Soanen, having initially prevaricated, once thirteen Bishops had been named before whom he might plead his cause—and against whom he himself had nothing to object—finally set out for Embrun, not without a profane retinue, and one that was not unarmed. But before he entered the city, he ordered it to be announced to the assembled group that he would never recognize them as judges. Subsequently, when asked by the Council whether that was indeed his Instruction, he did indeed deny that he had composed it, yet nonetheless openly professed that he entirely adopted, held, and approved it as his own, until he should be convinced of the errors which the Bishops had condemned in it. Indeed, the obstinacy of this man could not be overcome. For this reason, by the sentence of the Council, he was interdicted from every function, both Episcopal and Priestly, and a Vicar General was appointed for his diocese. It would be tedious to recount the outcries and tumults this scene provoked. Twelve Bishops protested against this sentence and brought a protestation to the King himself. Fifty advocates of the Parisian Court signed a consultation concerning the nullity of the sentence and the acts of the Council of Embrun. The clergy of Senez, supported by a crowd of monks and others, having repudiated the Vicar appointed by the Council, wished to obey no one other than Soanen’s previous Vicar, named la Porte. But the protestation of the Bishops was rejected by the King, the consultation of the advocates was suppressed by his authority, the outcries of the others were repressed by command, the Vicar la Porte was arrested, and thus quiet was restored to the whole province.
