§. 4.
*Appeal to a General Council.*

The thunders <note>a metaphorical reference to the threat of excommunication or formal condemnation</note> of the Vatican were already being prepared: Noailles was judged by the College of Cardinals itself to be unworthy of the purple <note>the red vestments symbolizing the dignity of a Cardinal</note>. Nevertheless, time was still given for repentance, arising from the hope that the Opponents had shown by having completed a certain scheme of doctrine. When this was not approved by those who accepted the Bull, they offered them a document in three columns, similar to that Jansenist one of old, in the central column of which were the very propositions of Quesnell, with the obvious sense on one side, and on the other some other Catholic sense, or at least one capable of excuse.

<summary>The page details the failure of negotiations between the Pope and the Jansenist-leaning opponents, specifically concerning their attempts to evade the Bull through alternative acceptance formulas and appeals to a General Council, ultimately leading to a final ultimatum from Clement XI.</summary>

¶ <term>Secundo</term> <gloss>Secondly</gloss>, the principal contains two orders outside the clergy, as in the book *De Periculosis* <gloss>On Dangerous [Orders]</gloss>, Book VI. ¶ <term>Primo</term> <gloss>First</gloss>, a religious who rashly discards the habit of his religion in schools or elsewhere is excommunicated by the letters of those who apostatize from the religious life, according to the decree *Si religiosus*. If a religious discards the habit for a shameful reason, such as going to a brothel at night, he falls into [the penalty]; it is otherwise if he does not discard the habit but hides it underneath or covers it with something else so he is not recognized, especially if he does so for a good reason, for instance, because it is hot and he does not want his religion to be known, provided he is still wearing the religious habit. Whoever discards it out of fear of thieves does not do so rashly. Nor are those excused who change their habit in schools so they do not appear to be religious. Whoever discards it for a moment out of lighthearted playfulness, to run or throw a stone, does not incur [the penalty], for it is probable he did not intend to violate the canons in such minor matters as to fall into such snares. ¶ <term>Secundo</term> <gloss>Secondly</gloss>, it is against religious who attend the studies of others without the counsel of their convent or without the permission of their superior or the greater part of their convent being granted for attending study, which is to be understood as when he goes to schools outside the town. However, it is not necessary for a gathering to be summoned for schools in the same town, and the license of the abbot is sufficient. ¶ <term>Item</term> <gloss>Likewise</gloss>, it is understood of those who actually reside in a convent, for those who are outside with the license of the abbot alone may go to schools. ¶ <term>Tertio</term> <gloss>Thirdly</gloss>, the principal contains those cases and instances of religious who are greedy or who defraud the churches of tithes owed to them, or if, when requested by those to whom it matters, they do not desist within a month, or if they have not made restitution for usurped or retained [tithes] within two months, they are suspended from their offices, administrations, and benefices, and those not holding such are excommunicated. ¶ <term>Uno</term> <gloss>One</gloss> case is that religious who [withhold] new or other tithes owed to churches, not pertaining to them for any legitimate reason.

Truly however</gloss>, sets forth two [things]: that monks or regular canons not having administration over others should not presume to present themselves at the courts of princes without the special license of their superiors. The text says that if they presume to present themselves at said courts so as to bring any damage to those superiors and monasteries, we will that they incur the sentence of excommunication <term>ipso facto</term> <gloss>by the fact itself</gloss>. Therefore, it is seen that two things are necessary to incur this excommunication, namely that the court is present, and that the cause is for the purpose of damaging the monastery or superior. Therefore, one is not bound by the mere act of leaving the cloister for this cause. The second case concerns monks <term>infra septa monasterii</term> <gloss>within the enclosure of the monastery</gloss> who bear arms without the license of their abbots. The text says this. Indeed, <term>Johannes Andreae</term> <gloss>John of Andrea, a famous canonist</gloss> says upon the word "bearing," that one coming from the outside to the cloister with arms, not intending to hold them, nor holding them by way of carriage, does not appear to be bound, and the word is [understood] with effect. The fifth principal [section] is against those who impede the visitors of nuns in their visitations through the modes stated in the <term>Clementines</term>, regarding the status of the clergy, chapter two, at the end. Unless they repent <term>munti</term> <gloss>mentally/in mind</gloss>, the gloss of <term>Johannes Andreae</term> suggests it is necessary that the impediment precedes and the warning follows. The sixth principal [section] regarding religious houses, chapter one, in the <term>Clementines</term>, contains two cases. The first condemns the status of the <term>Beginae</term> <gloss>Beguines</gloss> and excommunicates those following it or newly adopting it.
